events.title: Airlines waive change fees ahead of nor'easter as flight disruptions trickle in
events.summary: U.S. airlines kept most schedules intact ahead of the nor'easter that hit the Northeast U.S. this weekend. United Airlines, American Airlines and JetBlue Airways said customers can change flights without paying extra fees or fare differences if they were in the storm's projected path. Flight disruptions lingered around the Northeast on Sunday as the nor'easter continues to bring heavy rain and high winds to the Northeast U.S. Around 200 flights in and out of Boston were canceled on Sunday, about 15% of the day's schedule, while another 260 were canceled on Saturday, according to FlightAware. Dozens of others were delayed at major New England and New York-area airports. Carriers will often cancel a chunk, if not most, of their schedules during severe winter storms or hurricanes to ensure planes, passengers, and crews aren't out of place, but airlines kept most of the schedule in tact ahead of the nor'easter, with delays far fewer than other major storms. American Airlines , United Airlines , Delta Air Lines , and JetBlue Airways said customers can change flights to a range of airports in the New York City area, Boston, and smaller New England airports without paying a change fee or fare difference if they can fly anytime before the middle of next week. The weekend disruptions followed an equipment outage on Monday that forced carriers to cancel hundreds of flights bound for the New York area and Philadelphia. events.title: Iran's foreign minister keeps indirect talks with the U.S. open; Iranian navy claims capture of underwater drone
events.summary: Iran says reopening the Strait of Hormuz depends on the U.S. meeting Tehran’s conditions, while Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said a negotiated solution remains possible. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed it captured a U.S. Remus 600 unmanned underwater vehicle. U.S. President Donald Trump has rejected Iran’s most recent proposal and told aides he views renewed U.S. bombing after the midterm elections as likely, The Wall Street Journal reported. Iran is sticking to its position that it would only reopen the crucial Strait of Hormuz if its conditions are met, despite a rebuke from U.S. President Donald Trump , while a senior Iranian military leader stressed his country's readiness to continue fighting. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps on Sunday claimed that it seized an autonomous U.S. submarine. "Our conditions are clear; any progress toward the opening of the Strait of Hormuz is contingent upon the fulfillment of these conditions, and we will not back down from them," Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in a post on his Telegram channel translated by Google. "During our meetings with mediators, these conditions were fully conveyed, explained, and elaborated upon, and the mediators, in turn, relayed them to the American side," he said on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. Trump told reporters Saturday that he has rejected Iran's latest conditional proposal for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, through which about a fifth of the world's oil supplies moved before the start of the war. "They made a proposal but I rejected it." The Wall Street Journal quoted unnamed U.S. officials as saying that Trump told aides he expects to resume bombing Iran after November's midterm elections. Araghchi on Friday had proposed reopening the strait and resuming nuclear talks with the U.S. within seven days if the Trump administration accepts its conditions. In his latest statement, Araghchi said intermediaries between the U.S. and Iran have yet to relay a formal response from Trump to Tehran. "Only a negotiated solution can break this deadlock," he said. Tehran's conditions include a halt to what it calls U.S. "acts of aggression," an end to the naval blockade and economic warfare, and the release of Iranian assets, Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said last week. Iranian military leaders continued to underline their readiness to continue the war, which began on Feb. 28 with U.S. and Israeli air strikes on the country. "The war is not over," the Iranian Student News Agency quoted Iran's army commander-in-chief, Amir Hatami, as saying. "We have won, but we must consolidate this victory, and the aggressor enemy, who has suffered heavy blows, must continue to be prepared to receive heavy blows from the soldiers of our beloved Iran," he said. Meanwhile, the IRGC navy claimed Sunday to have captured an American underwater drone in the Strait of Hormuz. "IRGC Navy forces successfully captured an advanced unmanned underwater vehicle (UUV) belonging to the U.S. terrorist army," the Tasnim News Agency said in a Telegram post quoting the IRGC. It described the vehicle as a Remus 600 unmanned underwater vehicle and added that it has been handed over to the force's specialists for data recovery. "The IRGC Navy firmly declares that the Strait of Hormuz is closed [to unauthorized traffic]," it said. U.S. Central Command did not immediately respond to CNBC's emailed request for comment. The war has severely restricted energy shipments out of the Middle East, sending oil prices soaring and raising concerns about accelerating inflation globally. But crude prices posted a sharp drop for the week as Tehran and Washington held discussions on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly. West Texas Intermediate dropped 2.3% to close at $92.41 per barrel. Brent , the international benchmark, declined 2.1% to settle at $104.32. U.S. crude finished the week 7.9% lower while Brent was flat. WTI is up nearly 61% year to date, while Brent crude is more than 71% higher over the same period.

events.title: ‘Better deal’: What’s behind Trump’s rejection of Iran’s truce offer?
events.summary: Experts say Trump sees economic sanctions as key to extracting more concessions but he risks losing leverage. Donald Trump has rejected Iran’s latest proposal to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz as experts say the United States president believes Washington has more to gain by waiting than by accepting Tehran’s terms at this moment. “I reject their proposal,” Trump told reporters on Saturday, arguing that Iran wants an agreement because it is “losing so badly”. list 1 of 3 Pezeshkian says Iran ‘no longer trusts talks with Washington’ list 2 of 3 Trump rejects Iran’s seven-day roadmap to end war and reopen Hormuz list 3 of 3 Iraq seeks US exemption from ban on Iranian flights “They want to make a deal, and I think that’s fine,” Trump said. “I’d like to make a deal too. But that deal would not be acceptable.” On Sunday, Iranian ⁠⁠Foreign ⁠⁠Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran had ⁠⁠seen the initial reaction from ‌‌Trump to its proposal but had yet to receive a response through ⁠⁠mediators. In the latest diplomatic efforts, Qatar has played a role in mediating talks between Iran and the US on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly meeting in New York. Iran’s seven-day proposal included Washington lifting its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waiving sanctions on Iranian oil sales, releasing an estimated $12bn in frozen Iranian assets and observing a wider regional ceasefire, including in Lebanon and Yemen. Iran would then reopen the Strait of Hormuz and begin negotiations with Washington on a final agreement. The latest proposals are similar to the June memorandum of understanding (MoU) the two countries signed. But the MoU collapsed last month due to differences on the terms of the deal, which resulted in an escalation in attacks, particularly in and around the Strait of Hormuz, which essentially remains under Iranian blockade. According to experts, Trump’s rejection suggested that while both sides continue to publicly leave the door open for diplomacy, they remain far apart over who should make the first concessions. “Trump’s calculation looks fairly straightforward. He believes the combination of the naval blockade and economic isolation is finally squeezing Iran hard enough that Tehran’s latest proposal is evidence of weakness rather than an offer Washington needs to seize,” Andreas Krieg, associate professor at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera. His public argument that Iran is “losing badly” is important because it suggests he thinks time is improving the US bargaining position, Krieg said. A key part of Trump’s calculation appears to be a belief that the economic pressure on Iran has not yet run its course. The Trump administration has escalated economic pressure on Tehran, tightening its naval blockade while imposing sanctions targeting Iranian oil revenues and threatening secondary sanctions against countries doing business with Tehran. Last week, the US imposed aviation sanctions on Iran, disrupting flights. This came weeks after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced an economic pressure campaign against Iran, promising to target Tehran’s financial interests across the world. Richard Weitz, a senior nonresident associate fellow at the NATO Defence College, told Al Jazeera that the White House may believe it can “wait a bit and get better terms”. There is also concern in Washington about Iran’s proposed sequencing, he said. Therefore, Weitz said Washington may be calculating that “economic pressure over time will induce the Iranian government to make more concessions”. “This is what occurred arguably a decade ago, leading to the 2015 Iran nuclear deal as the Iranian government decided it [the US] needed to end the economic sanctions in return for making concessions on its nuclear programme,” he added. It is, therefore, possible that “we could see the same kind of trade-off in the coming months”. However, waiting for a deal also carries considerable political risk for the US president, experts said, because his Republican Party could lose November’s midterm elections. A late August Reuters/Ipsos poll suggested 63 percent of Americans opposed the US-Israel war on Iran while 31 percent supported it. Rising fuel and transportation costs could also feed into broader cost-of-living concerns before the elections. The problem for Trump is that time does not only increase pressure on Iran, Krieg said. “The gamble is that time cuts both ways,” he noted. With the midterms approaching, Trump does not want to appear to lift the blockade, waive oil sanctions and release Iranian assets simply to regain access to a waterway that Iran itself disrupted, Krieg said. “But every additional week also means elevated energy prices, continued military exposure and mounting pressure on Gulf partners.” The essential closure of the Strait of Hormuz has disrupted oil and gas flows from the Gulf nations, which depend on energy exports to finance their budgets.

events.title: Swiss voters set to reject tighter neutrality rules in referendum
events.summary: About 71 percent of voters oppose initiative to impose stricter limits on neutrality, projection suggests. Swiss voters appear to have overwhelmingly rejected a proposal to impose stricter constitutional limits on the country’s longstanding neutrality. About 71 percent voted against the initiative in a referendum on Sunday, according to a projection by the polling institute GFS Bern for the Swiss public broadcaster SRG. list 1 of 2 Iran shifts trade north to Caspian Sea as war impairs Strait of Hormuz list 2 of 2 Switzerland’s neutrality vote is asking the wrong question The result would preserve the government’s ability to impose sanctions and cooperate with NATO , the transatlantic military alliance whose members include most of Switzerland ’s larger neighbours, rather than lock those choices into a narrower constitutional definition of neutrality. The initiative sought to define Swiss neutrality as “perpetual and armed”. It would have barred Switzerland from joining or cooperating with military and defence alliances unless the country was under attack or an attack was imminent while allowing sanctions against states at war only when approved by the United Nations Security Council. Pro Switzerland, a group that campaigns for national sovereignty, organised the initiative, which was backed by the right-wing Swiss People’s Party (SVP), Switzerland’s largest party. Supporters argued that joining European Union sanctions against Russia and expanding security cooperation with NATO had weakened the country’s traditional neutral role. The Swiss government, parliament and nearly all major parties opposed the proposal, saying it would leave the country less able to respond to international crises. SRG said it projected about 29 percent support for the initiative. The argument over neutrality sharpened after Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 . Switzerland largely adopted EU sanctions against Moscow, prompting criticism from Russia and from supporters of stricter neutrality, who said the Swiss government was taking sides. Switzerland has been internationally recognised as neutral since 1815, and neutrality has formed part of its federal constitutional framework since 1848. Current policy still allows the country to cooperate with other states on security and to join sanctions while remaining outside military alliances. The vote, therefore, centred less on whether Switzerland should remain neutral than on how much freedom its government should retain in applying that principle as Europe’s security environment changes.

events.title: Fixing transportation issues is key to getting more workers into US submarine yards and keeping them, Navy official says
events.summary: One program has provided nearly $200,000 for transportation via gas cards and bus passes, the office said. US Navy Photo by John Narewski Transportation to submarine yards can be a hiring challenge for the US Navy. Programs have offered workers gas cards and bus passes to make commuting easier. The Navy is looking at local barriers as it races to expand the submarine workforce. Beyond pay, work-life balance, and scheduling, there are other basic challenges affecting the US submarine workforce, including how workers get to the job, a Navy official overseeing workforce concerns shared. The Navy's Submarine Industrial Base Program Office says it, along with its federal and state partners, has observed success in addressing region-specific problems, like transportation, that can be make-or-break for attracting new workers . Regional teams have been critical in examining the particular workforce needs around submarine construction and repair yards. Erica Logan, the office's director of workforce, told Business Insider earlier this year that her team looks at local factors, including education, demographics, unemployment, and cost of living. Transportation is also part of the assessment. "What does the transportation system look like? Is it a very rural area where there may not be transportation?" Logan said. "How would we get folks there? What could we do to help a supplier that lives in an area like that?" The office, she said, has supported several transportation pilots with bus systems to make it easier for submarine workers to get to and from work. These programs have prompted further questions about free bus passes and van pools. "I think we've done a lot in that area using this regional approach to really just get a good understanding of what that region has," Logan said. The Navy's Submarine Industrial Base Program Office is working on rebuilding the network of suppliers, builders, and manufacturers that construct Navy submarines . As part of the broader efforts to fix decades-old shipbuilding problems in the US, the office has focused on attracting and retaining workers, as well as addressing everything from pay and work-life balance to problems unique to individual communities. In one example provided by the office, General Dynamics Electric Boat partnered with the Rhode Island Public Transit Authority to provide direct service to the Quonset Point shipyard. Ridership has more than doubled year over year, the office said, and it came at no cost to the Navy. In another, the Hampton Roads Workforce Council provides workers with gas cards and bus passes to help them get to work. Since September 2023, the Hampton Roads Maritime Training System program within the council has provided nearly $200,000 in transportation assistance, funded through grants, donations, and the Virginia state government. Housing is also a challenge. The office hasn't funded permanent housing or related subsidies for shipyard or supplier workers. Instead, its efforts involve state and local engagement to expand affordable housing, as well as partnerships with specific yards or vendors. Some initiatives specifically support trainees. For instance, the Accelerated Training in Defense Manufacturing program in Danville, Virginia, offers students housing during their 16-week training. The program quickly trains candidates in manufacturing skills and trades to create a sustained flow of workers for jobs in naval shipbuilding and the submarine industrial base. Addressing these issues, along with competitive pay and benefits, is key to recruiting and retaining the workers that the Navy needs to meet its shipbuilding goals . Over the next 10 years, the service estimates it'll need to hire 250,000 skilled workers to account for the expected attrition and retirement in the workforce. events.title: I'm a dietitian who specializes in weight loss. Here are 4 fiber- and protein-rich breakfasts I eat when I'm tired of eggs.
events.summary: As a dietitian, I have a few go-to breakfasts in my rotation when I want to start my day with protein and fiber. Vanessa Imus I'm a dietitian who eats eggs often. When I need a change, I pick these easy, nutritious breakfasts . I focus on breakfasts with enough protein and fiber to help me stay full through the morning. Overnight oats, yogurt parfaits, smoothies, and avocado toast are my favorites. As a dietitian, eggs are a staple in my typical breakfast routine — and for good reason. They're high in protein, I really enjoy them, and they're fairly cheap. Plus, they're quick and easy to make, which is essential as a working mom of three. I typically pair them with vegetables and whole-grain toast or fruit for a more complete and filling meal. That way, I get plenty of fiber, protein, vitamins, and minerals first thing in the morning. Every now and then, though, I like to switch it up. Here are my non-egg go-to breakfasts that are easy to prepare and still fit into a balanced diet without falling short on protein and fiber. It takes me 5 minutes to whip up a batch of overnight oats that gives me 4 days' worth of breakfasts Overnight oats can be made in batches. Vanessa Imus I typically start with a basic recipe of 2 cups of oats, 2 ½ cups of milk (sometimes I use soy milk), ¼ cup of chia seeds, and 1 serving of protein powder. From there, I adapt by adding peanut butter, chocolate chips, and pecans, or blueberries, strawberries, and almond butter. There are so many variations of overnight oats online; everyone can find something that fits their taste buds. Oats are a great source of soluble fiber, which can help reduce elevated LDL, or "bad," cholesterol and support digestive health. Adding nut butter gives this breakfast healthy fats that help support vitamin absorption and make it more satisfying. Each serving of this pudding usually provides me with just over 20 grams of protein and more than 10 grams of fiber, both of which help make this more filling and support steadier blood sugar. (Notably, this varies based on the protein powder and add-ins I use.) This breakfast also helps me reduce sugar cravings later in the day. It doesn't get much easier than a yogurt parfait Yogurt parfaits are easy to customize. Vanessa Imus I love that this breakfast requires minimal ingredients and can be tailored to any food preferences. I start with 2 tablespoons of granola, then layer on some fresh or frozen fruit — berries are my favorite since they're a great source of fiber. Next, I add about ⅔ cup or 6 ounces of a high-protein plain and unsweetened yogurt, like Greek yogurt or a Greek-style yogurt alternative. Then, I sprinkle on another 2 tablespoons of granola and some more fresh or frozen berries. This recipe can provide about 15 to 20 grams of protein (or more), depending on the yogurt and granola you use, along with several grams of fiber from the berries and granola. I suggest comparing granola brands and choosing one that's lower in added sugars and has at least a couple of grams of fiber — bonus if it has at least a few grams of protein as well. I'm so glad I tried this smoothie made with beans … and I promise it doesn't taste like beans You would never believe this smoothie contains beans. Vanessa Imus I was a little wary when my mom shared a variation of this recipe with me, but I tried it anyway, and am so glad I did. This smoothie recipe uses ½ a cup of white beans, which adds 7 to 8 grams of protein and about 5 to 8 grams of fiber, depending on the beans used. It's pretty hard to beat that in a single food. Beans are a nutritional powerhouse and something many Americans don't eat enough of. They are the perfect package of protein and fiber. To make this smoothie tasty and beautiful, I add 1 cup of frozen berries, ½ frozen banana, 1 cup of milk or soy milk, and a scoop (about 2 Tablespoons) of Greek yogurt to the ½ cup of white beans and blend until smooth. Altogether, my smoothie usually has just over 20 grams of protein and can approach 20 grams of fiber, depending on the add-ins I use. It's satisfying enough to let me easily skip a morning snack and stay full all morning. Plus, the berries provide vitamin C, which can help support one's immune system . Chicken sausage with avocado toast keeps me full all morning I like adding greens to my avocado toast. Vanessa Imus Avocado toast maintains its popularity for good reason: It's tasty and full of nutrients like fiber, potassium, and heart-healthy fats. I love to sprinkle mine with a popcorn-blend seasoning, then top it with fresh arugula. Depending on your bread and how much avocado you use, this alone could get you 5 to 10 grams of fiber to start the day. Since I often recommend that people trying to manage their weight aim for 15 to 20 grams of protein per meal, I like pairing the toast with a few high-protein mini breakfast-sausage links . Adding fruit on the side, like half a sliced apple, helps round out the meal with a little sweetness, plus extra fiber, vitamin C, and antioxidants. This combo makes this meal extra satisfying and keeps me from getting hungry again an hour later. When I prepare this meal with my bread and add-ons of choice, it typically has about 20 grams of protein and 6 to 8 grams of fiber. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: I'm a matchmaker who charges up to $250,000. My clients want partners who are driven, but flexible.
events.summary: Matchmaker Sameera Sullivan works with men willing to pay $100,000 or more to find their partner. Photo credit: Jules Slütsky Sameera Sullivan has run a matchmaking business since 2013. Clients pay her up to $250,000, with the fee due before their first dates. She says dating apps have made people too picky, and she pushes back on client preferences. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Sameera Sullivan . It has been edited for length and clarity . As far back as high school, I loved giving people dating advice . My mom could see that I had real skill, and she encouraged me. Yet, I didn't even know that matchmaking could be a business. Then, in 2012, I was recruited by a matchmaking agency. Before then, I'd studied psychology and worked in education and defense. The agency thought that background would make me good at helping others find love. When I started matchmaking, I knew I'd found what I was supposed to do. But I didn't like the way the agency operated, so I decided to go out on my own. Since then, I've personally matched more than 100 couples. I focus on quality, not quantity, but my results speak for themselves, and my clients are willing to pay for my expertise . Most pay between $100,000 and $150,000. But some — the really picky, specific ones — pay $250,000. I put a lot of work in up front, so they pay before we get started. Some successful men struggle to choose a partner All my clients are men , most in their 40s and 50s. I think of them in two groups: some are bad pickers, who have just never been great at choosing a partner. The others are coming out of a divorce. Those guys know what they want and what they don't. No matter what type of guy a client is, we do a lot of psychological work and neuroscience coaching. I ask about their past relationships, identify their personality type, and help them better understand themselves so they can see red, yellow, and green flags while they're dating. I have a database of about 22,000 women who are willing to be matched with my clients. I generally show the client about 15 profiles. From there, we work together to choose three women for them to go on dates with. Sameera Sullivan and her husband, Tim. Courtesy of Sameera Sullivan My clients want women with purpose, but flexibility Understanding what will make a relationship work takes a blend of skills. It's part empathy, part rationalization, and a little common sense. The men I work with are extremely successful and wealthy. They don't typically care about a woman's finances, but they want her to have something of her own that she's passionate about. They're willing to take care of their partner, but they don't want someone who will mooch off them. At the same time, they're looking for a partner who is flexible about integrating into their lives. Most of these guys are very established where they are. Still, that's not always the case. With one of the couples I matched recently, the man is moving interstate to where his partner lives. His lifestyle allows him to be flexible for her. I think about how a couple's lifestyles and ambitions will match Each client is a unique search. I have employees whose full-time job is recruiting women, and we use proprietary software to do so. I find women on LinkedIn and at events; they also apply directly to my network. Right now, one of my clients is 44. He's ambivalent about having kids — most of my clients aren't looking to have more children. He wants a woman who is not necessarily subservient, but who is softer than he is. I have to be careful about the types of profiles I show him, because he's not looking for someone who is very career-oriented. Other clients are looking for new adventures together. One of my couples is opening a gym together, building off the woman's physical therapy and nursing background. Another couple — a man in construction management and a woman who owns a photography business — plan to raise cattle at a vacation home they just purchased. I help clients be more open-minded The clients who pay me $250,000 are the most picky and, therefore, difficult to match. It might be a guy in his 70s, looking for a woman in her 40s. Once, I had a client say that his partner had to have an Ivy League degree. You can bet I push back on things like that. I argue and challenge my clients, and they usually thank me for it. They're willing to listen, because they've hired me for my expertise. The women are sometimes less willing to be flexible, especially regarding height and age. Dating apps have made it more difficult for people to find their partner, because there's so much out there. On apps, the true significance of a relationship gets lost as people check boxes. You might quickly look at a profile and say, "He's not my type," without considering the connection you might have in person. People get in their own way. What does it matter if you're into brunettes, but the woman you really click with is blonde? Or, if you want to meet someone in Manhattan, but the right guy lives across the river in Jersey? You've got to be open-minded to love. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Floods and landslides kill at least 56 people in India, 12 in Nepal
events.summary: Authorities report increasing death toll over three days as rivers rise above danger levels across parts of neighbouring countries. Heavy rainfall has triggered floods and landslides that have killed at least 56 people in the northern Indian state of Uttar Pradesh in recent days while 12 people have been reported dead in neighbouring Nepal. Hrishikesh Bhaskar Yashod, Uttar Pradesh’s relief commissioner, said on Sunday that India’s most populous state had registered 66.5mm (2.6 inches) of rain from Friday to Sunday morning, compared with a normal 7.6mm (a quarter of an inch) for the period. list 1 of 3 Nepal’s leader labels devastating flood a ‘warning to the world’ list 2 of 3 Photos: Heavy rains and flooding in Bangkok force thousands into shelters list 3 of 3 Hurricane Polo lashes Mexico as Nolo strengthens near Hawaii The deaths, in addition to 46 injuries, were reported during a spell of “exceptionally heavy rain that has affected much of Uttar Pradesh”, according to the commissioner’s office. More than 1,000 houses were damaged after “a depression over the Bay of Bengal moved inland and intensified rainfall across the region,” it added. Home to more than 240 million people, Uttar Pradesh is frequently hit by rain and thunderstorms during the annual monsoon season from June to September. In India’s eastern state of Odisha, more than 70,000 people living in low-lying areas were evacuated after rivers rose due to heavy downpours, the NDTV news network reported. The rains have damaged bridges and culverts, forcing officials to shut down Devkund, a popular tourist spot in the state. Separately, India’s Central Water Commission said 30 river-monitoring stations across seven states were in a “severe situation”. Major rivers that flow through India, including the Ganga, Gandak, Kosi, Bagmati and Narmada, had risen above danger levels. In Nepal, where a devastating flood in late August killed more than 1,400 people and left thousands missing, a new wave of flooding and landslides has killed at least 12 people since Thursday, according to officials, with several others missing. Authorities warned of possible flash floods in 49 of the country’s 77 districts, with more than half facing high flooding or flash-flooding risks as water levels in major rivers and tributaries continued to rise. Power supplies have been disrupted in the Manang, Mustang, Myagdi and Baglung districts, with authorities working to ⁠restore electricity, officials at the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation said. Flooding of the Rahuganga River damaged the structure and transmission-line towers of a 40-megawatt hydropower project, Water Resources and Energy ⁠Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha said. Shanti Mahat, a spokesperson for the National ⁠Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, said Rasuwa and Nuwakot, areas hit by ⁠last month’s deadly floods, should remain “alert” but were not currently considered high-risk areas.

events.title: At NFL games this season, drone defense tech aims to bring down disruptions
events.summary: The Jacksonville Jaguars' new drone defense system is set to go live on Sunday ahead of the team's game against the New England Patriots. The NFL told CNBC it recorded 10,852 drone violations over stadiums between 2021 and 2025. Drone defense companies are seeking to keep pace with the rapid advancements in technology, and say more regulation over the industry is needed. As the NFL season begins, a new kind of defensive strategy is taking shape: Stopping drone disruptions. Last month, the Jacksonville Jaguars became the first NFL team to publicly announce an agreement with a drone defense company, seeking to protect against interruptions or security threats. The company, Ondas -owned Sentrycs, will control the skies in and around EverBank Stadium, home of the Jaguars, during game days. A representative for Sentrycs told CNBC the system will be activated for the first time on Sunday before the Jaguars' game against the New England Patriots. "As drones become increasingly accessible, we recognized the importance of moving beyond detection and adding an effective mitigation capability to our security strategy," said Jaguars Director of Events and Facilities Security Bobby Lyle in an August news release . The NFL, which is now on Week 3 of its 2026 regular season, told CNBC that it recorded 10,852 drone violations near stadiums between 2021 and 2025. Only a few of those resulted in disrupted games. In 2025, a playoff game in Baltimore between the Ravens and the Pittsburgh Steelers was paused due to a drone flying overhead. The stadium saw a similar incident in 2023. While the league previously had the capacity to identify and track drones near its 30 stadiums, evolving technology allows for the mitigation of threats by intercepting the communication link between an operator and the drone, taking control, and landing the aerial vehicle. Sentrycs said it recently signed deals with two other NFL teams, though CNBC could not confirm which franchises. Earlier this month, in tandem with Major League Baseball, the NFL sent a letter to the Department of Homeland Security arguing more resources are needed to protect fans and players from drones during competition. "Unauthorized drone activity presents an ongoing and growing challenge," the letter said. Sentrycs was one of several firms contracted to stop drone disruptions during the FIFA World Cup this past summer, which took place across 104 matches in the U.S., Canada and Mexico. The FBI reported about 700 instances of intercepting a drone during the four-week tournament. "What surprised us the most was the sheer number of drones in the air at one time," said Ondas founder and CEO Eric Brock. The federal government provided state and local authorities about $250 million in funding before the World Cup for drone defense. Now, those resources and improvements made ahead of the tournament can benefit other big, in-person events like concerts or festivals. "Nobody worried about this a few years ago. Now everyone has to worry, and it's happening very fast," said Jason Moore, Sentrycs' general manager for the U.S. and Canada. Drone defense operators must take special classes to become certified through a federal program. The systems require both hardware and software. Once equipment installation is complete, operators detect threats through optical systems including radar and thermal technology. Sentrycs also uses radio signals for detection. "The system allows for the operator to detect and then take over the drone's controls and to move it out of the way and land safely," Moore said. The system is also capable of using radio frequencies to find the pilot of a drone and alert police to their exact location. With officers on patrol, response time from the moment of detection to when a law enforcement officer could be at the scene of the operator can be as little as two minutes, according to Brock. While some experts cite the threat of civilian drones being equipped to deliver explosives or chemical or biological agents, authorities and defense executives say the more common risk is annoyance and interruption. "In most cases drones are operated by people either not paying attention to or ignoring the rules," said Kristian Brost, general manager of Robin Radar USA, which was also contracted to help with drone security during the World Cup. Robin Radar, headquartered in the Netherlands, operates equipment at two dozen European airports. About a dozen large European airports have been forced to temporarily suspend flights due to drone incursions in the last year, according to findings by the European Commission and various media reports. "Most drones weren't nefarious, but they still pose a threat and must be detected and taken down," said Brost, who served in the U.S. Marine Corps in Iraq during the opening stages of the 2003 war, working with emerging military technologies.

events.title: A NATO defense minister warns that the alliance needs to learn how to disperse weapons production before it's at war
events.summary: NATO member Latvia wants to learn from how Ukraine makes weapons more dispersed and underground and industry's close relationship with soldiers. Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images A NATO defense minister wants his arms makers to work with Ukrainian ones and learn. This includes how they work across multiple sites during wartime to avoid devastating attacks. "Our industry is a peacetime establishment," Latvia's defense minister said. NATO militaries need to learn how to disperse weapons production, as Ukraine does, before entering a war to preserve their ability to keep producing while under attack, a senior defense official advised. Raivis Melnis, the defense minister of Latvia, an alliance and EU member state bordering Russia, told Business Insider that industry in the West might not be ready to operate as it would need to in wartime. Ukrainian arms makers split up manufacturing across multiple sites, operate underground, and even move around to prevent a single successful Russian strike from having a huge impact on their operations. But in Europe, many companies run projects from larger factories, which could become a single point of failure. "Our industry is a peacetime establishment" that has been built under conditions where "there is no threat," Melnis said. NATO companies work in a far more concentrated way, he said, and "the question is whether we are ready to produce the systems in different locations, dispersed, and how we organize that." He said this is why he encourages partnerships between Latvian and Ukrainian defense companies, so they can learn from how the Ukrainian companies operate , including how their systems are "built for war purposes." Ukraine has also demonstrated how a country "can provide that reassurance if, for instance, an industry site is destroyed." Kyiv offers compensation for some business properties damaged or destroyed in Russian attacks and is planning additional support. Ukrainian officials and company leaders have been pushing for Western companies to adopt a more disaggregated approach to prepare for the possibility of a wider conflict. Davyd Aloian, the deputy secretary of Ukraine's National Security and Defense Council, told Business Insider that the Russian threat to Europe is so substantial that companies across NATO should "definitely" start breaking up their production more. Mykyta Rozhkov, the chief business development officer at Ukrainian arms maker Frontline Robotics, told Business Insider that some alliance defense firms have sought Frontline's advice on dispersing manufacturing operations. The company, he said, has adapted to "endure the loss of any site." Any loss is still "painful," but the company survives. Operations are designed so it's "as easy as possible to move," he added. The companies making drones and other gear in Ukraine work across multiple sites, including underground, and are able to move far more easily than their Western counterparts. Diego Fedele/Getty Images Oleg, a company executive at Ukrainian drone maker TechEx, told Business Insider that "every day we are facing another level of threat from Russia trying to hit the factories." The company, he said, has to find "creative ways to switch the locations every couple of months to raise the level of security for our people, because, of course, you want to take care of the people and keep them safe." He said the company warns its international partners that their conventions are "slightly outdated." He requested that only his first name be used for security purposes. The CEO of Ukrainian-Estonian defense tech company Ark Robotics told Business Insider that his company makes different components at different sites, something he said is "necessary" even if it's not ideal. A single site is "the best way to do it," but, he explained, the company has to be "smart about it and not create a big enough target for it to attract too much attention or to disclose where our operations are happening." He said this should be the "default for defense-based manufacturing going forward," even outside Ukraine. Some companies are already taking heed. Estonian company Krattworks, which makes drones used by Ukraine, agreed with these assessments. Karmo Saar, the company's head of sales, told Business Insider that for Ukrainian companies, it "would be a lot more economical, cheaper, and better to run this operation in one big facility, but they cannot do that." "In Europe, we do that," Saar said. "And when the war strikes, I think we're going to be punished." Srđan Kovačević, the CEO of Croatian drone technology company ORQA, which has signed up to begin working in Ukraine , told Business Insider that it is "our deep philosophy that distribution is more resilient" in Ukraine. "Distributed systems are much more resilient to any disruption than concentrated systems, centralized systems," he said, noting that the thinking appears to be shifting across Europe. "This distributed nature actually reinforces resilience, even though there are economic downsides to it," he added. Latvia wants to learn from how Ukraine fights on the battlefield and the lessons its arms makers have learned. Yan Dobronosov/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images Latvia is one of the NATO countries most worried about a Russian attack or invasion and has been a vocal supporter of increased defense spending within the alliance, helping to arm Ukraine, and taking lessons from Ukraine's fight . These lessons are being fed into a new automated anti-drone defense wall and the acquisition of Ukraine-tested gear. Melnis wants Latvian firms to learn directly from Ukraine's battlefield experience and has announced a series of deals to deepen cooperation between the two countries' defense industries. He told Business Insider that he wants Latvia's companies to learn from Ukraine's "proven, combat-tested" systems and combine that with Latvia's "peacetime establishment, where our scientist engineers can work and can develop and bring those two together." Ukraine's wartime experience and understanding, he said, is something for which "you can't just sit in a normal office and build and simulate and create." Ukrainian companies, he said, work much more closely with front-line units than Western firms do. Ukraine's "military industry has established really close cooperation with the armed forces," he said. "We don't have such experience." "This is something I want to bring as well, that experience in," Melnis said, saying he wants to "take those best practices." Deterring Russia, he said, requires strong capabilities and also continued support for Ukraine. Russia wants "to destroy that support for Ukraine," he said. "Therefore, it is important for us to support, and we will be supporting Ukraine to build the victory." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Houses can be built on floodplains despite failing safety test, says high court
events.summary: Decision to allow development of 190 new homes in north Somerset sparks campaign for change in the law Houses can be built on floodplains even if they fail a crucial safety test, according to a high court judgment that will be of “immense interest” to developers across England and Wales. The ruling clears the way for a highly controversial development of 190 new homes on north Somerset’s floodplains, despite the site being in “flood zone 3a”, the highest level of flood risk before land is considered a functional floodplain. Ministers and experts are so disturbed by the decision that it was agreed at a flood resilience conference on Wednesday to campaign for a change in the law that would stop the ruling setting a national precedent. As a result, Tessa Munt, the chair of the flooding and flooded communities all-party parliamentary group (APPG), will now meet Matthew Pennycook, the housing and planning minister, to ask him to change the national planning policy framework (NPPF). “This is a dangerous and nationally significant exploitation of planning loopholes,” Munt said. “Tragically, we’ve lost the battle in north Somerset, but we need to change the framework as a matter of urgency, so this ruling doesn’t result in planners and developers across the country making similar speculative housing applications.” Charles Banner KC, who represented Persimmon Homes at the court case brought by the local council, agreed the decision was of national significance. His chambers, Keating Chambers, said the result was “hugely important”. “This decision will be of immense interest to the planning and development sector,” it added. Persimmon Homes won permission despite failing the “sequential test”, which is designed to be the ultimate barrier for floodplain development UK planning policy, after the inspector found 12 alternative sites at less risk of flooding. They also overcame heavy opposition from politicians, local and regional tiers of authority and locals – many of whom fear houses surrounding the site will be at increased risk of flooding. Munt said the high court judgment “flies in the face of everything insurers, lenders, Flood Re – a joint UK government and insurance industry initiative that makes the flood cover part of household insurance policies affordable – the Environment Agency and Defra are trying to do on a national policy level”. The Environment Agency objected to the development on flood risk grounds. But the high court agreed that even though the sequential test had failed, the inspector was entitled to consider the development’s wider benefits and whether it could be made safe for its lifetime when weighing the application. Annemieke Waite, North Somerset council’s cabinet member for planning and environment, accused Persimmon of exploiting a legal loophole. “We’re not being nimbys, we accept we need to build these homes,” she said. “But we don’t accept the establishment of a highly controversial legal precedent whereby vital local environmental protections can be overridden to build on floodplains across England and Wales.” Local people living around the site are distraught. With just a few hours’ notice, 51 residents converged at the site earlier this week to meet the Guardian’s photographer, many leaving work early to be there – and one coming straight from a hospital bed. “We represent everyone living in areas at risk of flooding in England and Wales,” said Sue Gardiner, whose living room window opens out over the site. “This ruling massively increases the likelihood of developers building up near you, without having to answer for your increased flood risk.” Gazing over the fields, Gardiner broke down. “I’m petrified,” she said. “Persimmon claims we’re not at any significant greater risk of flood, but no one else agrees: we’ve been refused by three major house insurers on the grounds of increased flood risk on the back of these plans. “Without insurance, our home – the home we worked hard throughout our lives to pay for so we could leave it to our children – could become unmortgageable, and then unsellable,” she said. “Thanks to Persimmon, our only asset could become a dangerous flood hazard for us – and a worthless inheritance for our children.” Richard Croucher, whose home also abuts the site, agreed. “The value of our home was supposed to fund our care when we get old,” he said. “Now we’ve got nothing for when we’re old and in need: that’s terrifying.” Persimmon Homes said: “Our proposals to deliver much-needed new homes in Yatton were subject to detailed scrutiny at a public planning inquiry before being approved by an independent planning inspector. “Flood risk was considered in detail through the planning process, including at the public inquiry by the inspector, before planning permission was granted.”

events.title: I moved countries for love in my late 40s. I had to rebuild my career, friendships, and identity.
events.summary: The author moved after being long distance. Courtesy of the author I moved from India to Austria for my partner in my late 40s. I left an established career, close friendships, and a life I'd spent decades building. Starting over taught me that reinvention is possible at any age. I was in a long-distance relationship when I moved from India to join my partner in Austria. I first met him four years earlier while doing what I loved best — introducing travelers to India as an Airbnb experience host. We connected instantly. Two years later, in the middle of the pandemic, we became life partners. After another gap for visa formalities, I joined him in Austria. Unlike most people who make this shift in their 20s, I was doing it in my late 40s. It was a difficult decision because I was at the peak of my career as a content creator at a New York-based agency and had built a life in a city I loved. Many people said it was a mistake. But today, after relocating during a pandemic, making a cultural transition into another country, learning a new language , and reestablishing my career in the most unconventional way, we have built a life we love. Our relationship is stronger My move to Austria during the pandemic was slow. While cross-border moves usually involve bureaucratic hurdles, the pandemic made them even more complex. The author moved in her 40s to be with her partner. Courtesy of the author But we prepared carefully and fulfilled all legal requirements. Facing uncertainty together made us more certain of our plans and drew us closer. It helped us build the resilience we needed for the path ahead. Home is something you build together, not a place where you are born One of the most difficult things I had to do was gather over 40 years' worth of belongings into a bag. Doing that showed me how to downsize my life to what really mattered. When I arrived in Austria, my partner's things were still in boxes in our new house. I added my suitcase to them and we unpacked everything we owned. We built our home by making it a space that reflected both our identities. It's never too late to start again The difficult part about moving later in life is rebuilding your old systems from scratch. Not just the big things like settling into a new home or finding a job, but also the small things like figuring out how public transport works or navigating bureaucracy in a new country . The author says it's never too late to start again. Courtesy of the author I rebuilt my old systems, from setting up a new bank account to getting an Austrian phone number, all with tremendous support from my partner. As an independent woman, I learned to be vulnerable and ask for support when I needed it. Thinking in a new language is life-changing I had already begun learning German before I moved. But for the first time, I was in a classroom where none of the other students knew English. But we did learn to speak to each other. Our adult language classroom helped me meet incredible people from around the world who were also relocating. Learning a new language with them made me a better communicator. Careers are connected to what you do, not where you live The biggest problem with leaving a country later in life is letting go of the professional identity you have established. I stepped down from leading the content practice at a New York agency and left behind my identity as a bestselling author in India. But the digital world helped me stay connected to both those identities. Instead of looking for employers, I looked for clients instead. I used my experience to become a content consultant to companies around the world, followed my passion as a travel writer, and published my first poetry anthology. Having a personal network matters The deep bond between my partner and me did not compensate for the loss of my friends and family back home. Unlike when you leave home earlier, I had built these friendships over the last four decades. My first friends were my partner's friends. But one of the best decisions I made was to join a local book club. Not only did it help me to keep reading, but it also gave me a chance to meet people with similar interests. You have to embrace your roots and wings I also had to find my balance between the two countries I now call home. I was still keenly aware of my home country's history and cultural traditions. But I also came to appreciate many things about being Austrian. As someone who had been an experienced host, I learned about Austrian history, culture, food, and traditions with the same enthusiasm. Embracing my new country helped me genuinely value and come to enjoy my new home. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Top Wall Street analysts like these 3 dividend stocks for steady income
events.summary: Stock markets remain volatile as investors weigh uncertainty in the Middle East, rising interest rates and concerns about the artificial intelligence (AI) trade. Given this volatile backdrop, investors seeking a stable income stream can enhance their portfolios with the addition of dividend stocks. In this regard, tracking recommendations of top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend stocks that are backed by strong financials. Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance. Integrated oil and gas giant Chevron ( CVX ) is the first dividend pick. Earlier this month, the company paid a quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share. At an annualized dividend of $7.12 per share, CVX offers a dividend yield of about 3.5%. After a meeting with senior leadership, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on CVX and raised his price target to $240 from $225. Among the key takeaways Mehta emphasized was that Chevron is building a solid pipeline of promising international exploration projects across Latin America, the Middle East, West Africa and the Eastern Mediterranean. In particular, he mentioned the focus on Venezuela, where Chevron expects to more than double gross production to 600 kbd from about 280 kbd by 2031, using three joint ventures. Mehta also noted Chevron's efforts to deploy new technologies, especially in shale and tight-oil operations. CVX is focused on boosting productivity and efficiency to maximize free cash flow, he added. Initiatives such as artificial lift optimization, AI and machine learning, and advanced chemical treatments are expected to improve recovery by about 10% in new wells. Consequently, capital spending per barrel in U.S. shale is projected to fall 25% in 2026, with total Permian spending dropping below $3.5 billion. Mehta also said that Chevron sees power as a growth opportunity and is using its U.S. natural gas portfolio, key equipment and partnerships to meet rising demand. Notably, Chevron recently signed a 20-year power purchase deal with Microsoft (MSFT) to supply 2.67 GW of behind-the-meter capacity. This project, called Kilby, is expected to see its first power delivery in 2028 and generate mid-teens returns and long-term cash flows. Mehta ranks No. 536 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 61% of the time, delivering an average return of 11.3%. See Chevron Statistics on TipRanks. Enterprise Products Partners ( EPD ) is a master limited partnership (MLP) that provides midstream energy services to producers and consumers of natural gas, natural gas liquids (NGLs), crude oil, refined products and petrochemicals. With a quarterly cash distribution of 56 cents per common unit ($2.24 per common unit annualized), EPD offers a yield of about 6%. Following a recent call with the company, RBC Capital analyst Elvira Scotto reiterated a buy rating on EPD with a price target of $42 . The analyst slightly lowered her estimates for the second half of 2026, citing margin and volume normalization, though demand dynamics remain strong. While the 5-star analyst expects a sequential decline due to normal seasonality and normalization following high spreads in the first half of the year, she still expects EPD to report another solid quarter (Q3 2026) and enter 2027 with a favorable setup. Ahead of Q3 earnings, Scotto expects investors to focus on export demand durability, EPD's ability to profit from spot cargo sales and growth in Permian volumes. Scotto continues to expect $150 million of common unit buybacks per quarter in the second half of 2026. She expects buybacks to increase to $200 million per quarter in 2027, as capex spending declines and free cash flow improves. In total, Scotto is bullish on EPD and views it as a core MLP holding that has both offensive and defensive characteristics. The analyst praised EPD's diverse asset base as ensuring stable cash flows. "Furthermore, the partnership's multi-year organic growth backlog helps provide visibility on long-term distribution growth," Scotto said. Scotto ranks No. 199 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 67% of the time, delivering an average return of 15.9%. See Enterprise Products Partners Financials on TipRanks. Brookfield Infrastructure Partners ( BIP ) operates a diversified portfolio of high-quality utilities, transport, midstream and data assets. The company declared a quarterly distribution of 45.5 cents per unit, payable on September 29. At an annualized distribution of $1.82, BIP offers a yield of 5.2%. Recently, BMO Capital analyst Devin Dodge reaffirmed a buy rating on Brookfield Infrastructure with a price target of $47 . The analyst cited improved visibility into BIP's growth and views its corporate simplification as a potential catalyst.

events.title: Wall Street money takes back over from small investors as driving force of the stock market
events.summary: After years on a big buying streak, retail traders appear to have been moving to the sidelines, data from Vanda Research shows. At the same time, big investors have held steady on stocks in the face of spiking Treasury yields. Institutional investors are taking the wheel in the stock market. After years on a big buying streak, retail traders appear to be moving to the sidelines. At the same time, data from Vanda Research shows that big investors have held steady on stocks in the face of spiking Treasury yields. "Institutional investors have been surprisingly resilient through this week's macro volatility," Viraj Patel, global market strategist at Vanda, wrote to clients on Friday. Options flows from institutional investors are around three times higher than a typical September, the data shows. Patel said that big money's flows have turned up over the past five sessions, despite the 10-year and 30-year U.S. Treasury yields climbing to their highest levels in more than a decade. He called that a "reasonably constructive signal for risk appetite" among institutional investors hidden in the broader story of de-risking. Patel said that institutional traders are buying select artificial intelligence plays amid the volatility. He pointed to Meta Platforms as a top pick in particular last week. Shares of the Facebook parent have surged almost 13% in the week following its debut of the Muse Charm device. Momentum has been building for the stock since Meta unveiled its Muse personal AI agent earlier this month. "Macro uncertainty isn't stopping risk-taking," Patel said. Instead, "it's making investors far more selective." Retail traders had a banner performance in 2025 , leading some to declare that they had shed the "dumb money" title. Their performance was credited in part with decisions to buy the dip during market declines in the wake of President Donald Trump's tariff rollout. But Goldman Sachs said retail investors' share of S&P 500 trading volume has trended down from its peak nearly a year ago. It's now more than three percentage points below the five-year average, the bank found. The S&P 500 is ended last week more than 1% higher despite the pressure from rising Treasury yields. That advance has pulled the benchmark into positive territory for the month.

events.title: Why the US-Iran war is working in China’s favour
events.summary: It must be unique for New York to host the president of a country at war with the US. But alongside Iran’s Masoud Pezeshkian, who is in town for the UN General Assembly , an even more important protagonist in the conflict visited Donald Trump: Chinese leader Xi Jinping . What does Beijing stand to gain from the US-Iran conflict ? It benefits from Washington’s distraction. While a third of the US Navy is occupied in a war with no clear end goal, the US squanders munitions and international respect alike. Meanwhile, China is free to expand its strength, deal with its own problems and pose as the responsible, rule-abiding superpower. The current “warm war” suits it just fine. With a strenuous and expensive US military effort, oil and other commodities are getting out of the Gulf in increasing amounts, although not to pre-conflict levels. That keeps up the domestic political pressure on the White House and means it cannot easily walk away. China has reportedly provided satellite imagery to the Iranians to help them target US bases. It has also supplied shipments with dual-use components that Iran could use to build missiles and drones. As with Russia’s war against Ukraine, China can simultaneously profit, make itself invaluable to a combatant, keep a conflict bubbling along, restrain full-scale escalation and maintain the facade of benevolent neutrality. In this vein, China does not want energy flows from the Gulf to be almost entirely cut, or for Iran to escalate, or return to large-scale, damaging attacks against regional infrastructure, as in March and April. It is a key investor across the Arab Gulf countries, much more than in Iran. It has large and expensive assets and many of its citizens live in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Oman and Iraq. The Bab Al Mandeb strait at the southern end of the Red Sea, under recent threat from Iran’s allies, the Houthis in Yemen, is a key conduit for Chinese goods to Europe. A Chinese naval base in Djibouti keeps watch over this strait. The GCC and Iraq are cumulatively far more important energy suppliers, customers and economic partners for China than Iran. Beijing does not need to choose between them. In 2023, it brokered a deal to restore diplomatic relations between Riyadh and Tehran, following the damaging drone and missile attacks on Saudi oil facilities in 2019. Some hoped it would intervene to prevent a repeat. In this year’s war, China might have quietly restrained Iran from trying to unleash more devastation on Saudi energy infrastructure, which would damage its own interests, but it has not emerged as a mediator. Staying out of the morass probably seems wise in Beijing now, though it does impose a hard limit on China’s diplomatic and security weight. It has to be careful not to appear a fair-weather friend, or worse, a two-faced one, in the Gulf. A return to the near-total blockade seen early in the war would hurt China’s key trading partners in Asia and Europe, notably energy-short Japan, South Korea and the Asean nations. Its export-dependent economy is limping; it does not want a global recession. But Beijing is the best-prepared major nation for such an energy crisis, if it continues at a restrained level. Unlike the US, now a major net exporter, it is the world’s largest importer of both oil and gas. However, its domestic coal resource base and its vast and growing renewable and nuclear sectors insulate its electricity system from gas shocks. It can be relatively flexible in its imports of liquefied natural gas, where Qatari shipments have been severely disrupted, because of its major gas pipelines from Russia and Central Asia. In turn, Moscow’s decision to torpedo its core European gas market has left it reliant on its giant eastern neighbour. Another ill-judged decision to go to war has contributed to Chinese ascendancy. Last year, almost as if Beijing foresaw what was coming, it accumulated huge strategic stocks of oil, which it has been gradually drawing down since the start of the war. Its state-directed energy system has proven a useful tool in meeting national priorities. It continues to electrify its road transport, gradually reducing its need for petroleum. And its juggernaut of a clean-tech sector continues to gain from the war. Six of the top seven electric vehicle makers worldwide are Chinese. It accounts for about 79 per cent of the world’s wind turbine market, 80 per cent of the global solar photovoltaic market, and 80 to 90 per cent of core components for lithium-ion batteries. Independent Chinese refiners did benefit from the opportunity to import cut-price Iranian crude. With the effective US maritime blockade, the last dribs of that are arriving. We still have to see whether China will help its friend weather the embargo, or somehow enable more Iranian oil to evade the stranglehold. After losing an ally in Venezuela in January, it will not want to see another leading oil exporter forced to bow to America. On August 24, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced an “Economic D-Day” against Iran. But notably, the tougher sanctions have not specifically targeted China, which remains Tehran’s key trading partner and essentially the only remaining customer for its oil. Some previous American measures have hit individual Chinese independent refineries and oil terminals, but none of the major or systemically important ones. China has enacted counter-sanctions, which would target companies complying with US restrictions, presenting them with a tricky choice. This resembles the European Union’s blocking statute, first introduced in 1996 and revived in 2018. But Brussels has never had the guts to wield this weapon seriously; Beijing will. It has leverage over the US, particularly in its ability to cut off rare-earth supplies. China thus has significant influence over the success of American sanctions against both Tehran and Moscow. Of course, things could still go wrong. Chinese petroleum stocks are not infinite, while the US’s mastery of shale oil and gas remains a huge strategic advantage. A breakthrough in nuclear fusion or artificial intelligence might turbocharge the US energy system. The regime in Tehran could collapse under the strains of war and sanctions, and hand the US another invaluable Middle Eastern ally. For all its strengths, China’s state-centric economy has serious long-term weaknesses. It cannot shrug off a severe shortage of oil indefinitely, in combination with its huge debt overhang, a real estate slump, an ageing workforce, and an over-reliance on exports in a suspicious world. Yet, as US secretary of state Madeleine Albright said in 1998, “We are the indispensable nation. We stand tall, and we see further than other countries into the future.” Now she might have been speaking from the Great Hall of the People by Tiananmen Square.

events.title: The British military is feeding a 'load of data' from the war in Ukraine into its next-gen Challenger 3 main battle tank
events.summary: The next-generation Challenger 3 tank is absorbing lessons from the war. Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land/Screengrab via YouTube Britain's next-generation main battle tank is being developed and enhanced amid the war in Ukraine. The new tank is a fully modernized version of the decades-old Challenger 2, which Ukraine operates. It will feature a digital overhaul and new weaponry that make it more compatible with NATO. As drones completely reshape how armored vehicles are used on the battlefield in Ukraine, the developers behind the British Army's next-generation tank are taking these lessons into account. Britain's Challenger 3 main battle tank is intended as a major upgrade over its predecessor, which is in service with both the British Army and the Ukrainian military. The new tank will feature a digital overhaul and new weaponry that make it more compatible with other NATO forces . "We're taking a load of data from Ukraine" and feeding it into the Challenger 3 development, a UK defense ministry spokesperson told Business Insider at an exhibition near London last week. The tank has a smart targeting system built primarily for combating enemy armor, but it can be adapted to detect hostile drones, a major threat on the modern battlefield. For protection, the tank is equipped with explosive reactive armor. New features for the Challenger 3 are modular, meaning they can be swapped in and out, the spokesperson said, adding that Britain has options for drone-related equipment that can be installed as needed. British Army officers told Business Insider at the UK defense industry exhibition that the UK is learning lessons from Ukraine, not only for the development of the Challenger 3, but for armored vehicles in general, like how they can remain survivable on a modern battlefield. The officers emphasized that the version of the new Challenger 3 tank that exists today is not a finished product; the core platform will continue to be improved to keep pace with changes in modern warfare. The Challenger 3 is the successor to the decades-old Challenger 2. Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land/Screengrab via YouTube In 2021, the UK defense ministry awarded Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land a $1 billion contract to upgrade roughly 150 Challenger 2 tanks , which entered service with the British Army nearly three decades ago and have seen combat in the Middle East and Ukraine. The new upgraded tanks, designated as Challenger 3s, were designed as digital fighting vehicles with state-of-the-art targeting, fire-control, surveillance, and survivability systems. One of the biggest changes is the addition of a 120mm L55A1 smoothbore main gun that fires NATO-standard ammunition , replacing the Challenger 2's rifled gun that used ammunition unique to Britain. Other improvements include a redesigned turret, better thermal imaging, enhanced armor, and upgrades to the tank's engine, suspension, and other key systems. There are seven Challenger 3 prototypes, and an eighth is in production. The tanks have already completed their first crewed live-firing trials and are undergoing additional testing before expected delivery next year, which was pushed back from 2025. The Challenger 3 is at the center of what British Army officers and officials describe as the new "20-40-40" model, a layered approach to armor operations designed to protect high-value assets such as tanks and helicopters by relying more on cheaper drones and robots . The defense ministry spokesperson said this approach was taken directly from Ukraine, where cheap drones worth hundreds of dollars have been able to destroy armored vehicles that cost millions. The 20-40-40 model underscores that while the war in Ukraine has raised questions about the utility of tanks and other armored vehicles on modern battlefields, British military leaders still see them as a core part of their strategy. events.title: Andy Burnham refuses to back third runway at Heathrow
events.summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has refused to say whether he backs a third runway at Heathrow after it emerged that the expansion of the London airport could be delayed by up to four years. Burnham - who, as Mayor of Greater Manchester, opposed the project - told Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg: "I think principally, it's a matter for London and Londoners." He added: "I think we ought to hear the voice of people there first. It's not right for me to just jump straight in on the back of the consultation." Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves had championed the runway to boost the economy, with a schedule to open by 2035 but Heathrow indicated on Saturday it may not be operational before 2039. As Manchester's mayor, Burnham had been against the project over concerns that it would delay investment in transport for the north. When he took office, he said he was "open-minded" about the scheme. As he prepared for his first annual Labour Party conference as prime minister, Burnham said: "There's a consultion but there are different views and you have to take those views seriously in coming to a decision." In response, Heathrow said: "We agree with the prime minister that local voices must be heard. We know from consistent polling over the last decade that communities support our plans for expansion and support is only growing over time." The project, estimated to cost £33bn, has attracted opposition from environmental campaigners and local resident groups as well as Mayor of London Sadiq Khan. A third runway would mean demolishing hundreds of homes, diverting rivers and rerouting a section of the M25 motorway through a tunnel. But it is estimated it would create 100,000 jobs and provide a major boost to the UK economy. The number of flights from the site, currently capped at 480,000 a year, could go up to 720,000, or nearly 2,000 a day on average. A new runway has been backed by the unions Unite and the GMB. Sharon Graham, Unite's general secretary said: "A third runway at Heathrow is essential and we need to get going with it. "This is more than just infrastructure. It's about investing in the workforce, securing the future of good, unionised jobs and a guaranteed market for UK steel." Earlier this weekend, Heathrow conceded that meeting the original deadline would be increasingly difficult without further steps to simplify the planning process. It said it hoped to secure planning permission by 2029 and then open the runway "within a decade". The Department for Transport said the timeline had "always been ambitious" and it would continue to work with stakeholders "at pace" on the matter. events.title: My husband has been going on the same family trip every year since he was a baby. Now, we get to bring our daughter.
events.summary: The author's husband goes to the same place every summer for a family reunion. Last year, their daughter joined for the first time. Courtesy of Riana Ang-Canning My husband's family goes to the same place every year for a family reunion. I started going with him in 2015, and last year, our daughter went for the first time. I'm excited to continue the family tradition with the next generation. Every year, my husband's family gathers on the Sunshine Coast of British Columbia, Canada, for a long weekend family reunion . They fish, swim, hike, roast marshmallows around the campfire, and catch up on the back deck. The weekend culminates in the annual horseshoe tournament, where the winners add their names to the trophy and we all celebrate with a potluck roast dinner . My husband, Colin, has been going up to the Sunshine Coast every year since he was a baby. There's a tree on the property that he planted in elementary school that now stands over 40 feet tall. I started attending with him in 2015, first as his girlfriend and then in 2022, as his wife. And now we get to share this annual family tradition with our daughter. Last year, our daughter joined the family trip for the first time In 2025, we got to bring our daughter up to the Sunshine Coast for the first time. Not only was it her first time joining the family trip, but at 5 months old, it was her first trip ever. It was so fun to bring our daughter along and to introduce her to my husband's extended family . We spent most of our trip out on the back deck, where our daughter lay on a blanket, entertaining her relatives. The fresh air even helped her sleep through the night! In between naps and nursing, we squeezed in a family hike and a quick swim. But overall, it was a very laid-back vacation with our baby. The couple enjoys seeing their daughter experience the Sunshine Coast. Courtesy of Riana Ang-Canning This year, with a toddler, it was a completely different trip When we headed back up to the Sunshine Coast in July 2026, we knew it was going to be a totally different trip than the year before. This time, we had an 18-month-old toddler who was on the move, eating full meals, and only napping once per day. It was a lot more work to keep up with our daughter this year. Colin and I were constantly checking that someone was with her and taking inventory of everything she might need (toys, snacks, a life jacket, a water bottle, etc.). But it was also a lot of fun. Last year, she wasn't crawling or walking . But this year, she was running across grass fields, sitting in her own child-size camping chair, and helping herself to snacks from the kitchen. My favorite part of this year's trip was seeing our daughter bond with her cousins. She was enamored by the big kids, and they totally took her under their wing. I loved watching her play piano with them and hold hands as they walked down trails together. We can't wait to continue this family tradition with the next generation When I first joined my husband's annual family trip in 2015, I knew I was so lucky to have this beautiful place to visit every year in the company of the nicest people. The Sunshine Coast became one of my favorite places in the world. And now the trip is that much more meaningful because we get to share it with our daughter. I love that we're passing on this family tradition to the next generation and that we'll be able to mark the years of her life in annual trips to the Sunshine Coast. This year, she was thrilled to meet the goats who live next door, go out on the boat to check crab traps, and blow bubbles with her cousins. I can't wait to see what she experiences on our trip next year! Read the original article on Business Insider
