events.title: Apple buried Copland 30 years ago. Now the failed OS boots in a browser
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters The final developer build offers a glimpse of the future Cupertino abandoned for NeXT Asahi fork embraces LLMs and lands Linux on the M4 Mac mini 1 day ago iPhone 18 Pro benchmark boosted by giving it a cold drink 2 days ago Skip the upgrade? iPhone 18 Pro aperture about as unrepairable as it gets, iFixit finds 5 days ago The vulnpocalypse rains iBugs down on Apple with record-setting number of patches 11 days ago Apple iPhone Duo makes developers think in folds 12 days ago Thirty years after Apple abandoned Copland, its doomed attempt to create a modern Mac operating system, a new emulator lets you try the final developer build in your browser. Copland was intended to replace Apple's System 7 with a PowerPC-native operating system built around a microkernel, protected memory, and preemptive multitasking for system services. Three unfinished developer builds – D7E1, D9, and D11E4 – are publicly known. Relatively few people outside Apple's developer community in the mid-1990s ever had the opportunity to use them. Now you can boot Apple Copland D11E4 in your browser and explore the unstable prerelease OS without installing anything. Developer Michael Steil , also known as Mist , made it possible with an experimental fork of the DingusPPC Power Mac emulator . Steil says the 11 patches that enable DingusPPC to boot Copland were written with AI assistance. The upstream project does not accept AI-assisted patches, so the fixes would have to be rewritten before they could be incorporated. Don't expect miracles. The emulator runs D11E4, the final build Apple distributed to developers, dating from June 1996. It remains very much unfinished: if the emulated system hits an assertion, it drops into a debugger and asks the user to continue manually. Apple CEO Gil Amelio had demonstrated Copland at the company's 1995 Worldwide Developers Conference , but the project never approached the stability required for release. Much of Copland existed as plans and documentation rather than finished code. In 2009, Steil assembled an extensive archive of that material in Apple Copland Reference Documentation . There was also a planned successor to Copland, codenamed Gershwin , but it remained nothing more than a plan. The modern Gershwin desktop we covered a year ago is a nod to that nonexistent OS. Anyone familiar with the classic Mac OS of the late 1990s will recognize parts of Copland, and for good reason. Copland overran so badly that Amelio recruited the late Ellen Hancock from IBM as Apple's chief technology officer and tasked her with getting the project back on track. After reviewing its progress, she instead recommended cancelling it and acquiring an operating system elsewhere. Apple considered several alternatives, including acquiring Be for BeOS and working with Sun on a system based on Solaris. It ultimately bought NeXT, bringing Steve Jobs back to the company along with NeXTSTEP. Hancock was later sidelined under Jobs and resigned in 1997. Apple acquired NeXT at the end of 1996, just months after cancelling Copland. The first developer release of its NeXTSTEP-based successor, Rhapsody , followed in 1997 – continuing the musical codenames, if not the code. Rhapsody evolved into Mac OS X Server 1.0 in 1999 and the consumer release of Mac OS X 10.0 in 2001. Replacing the Mac OS architecture took years. While that work continued, Apple folded some of Copland's more mature components into updates to its existing operating system. Mac OS 8 , released in 1997, gained Copland's Platinum interface and a PowerPC-native, multithreaded Finder. Its Appearance control panel supported themes, although Apple shipped only Platinum. Renaming what had been planned as Mac OS 7.7 also helped Apple end the clone program, whose licensing agreements covered System 7. Mac OS 8.1 followed in 1998 with HFS+, Apple's new format for larger disks. Later that year, Mac OS 8.5 became the first PowerPC-only release.

events.title: I spent $7,500 on a full-body checkup and cosmetic procedures in Turkey
events.summary: The author said he was unhappy with the medical care he was getting at home, so he used his airline miles to book a business class ticket to Turkey for care and cosmetic procedures. Courtesy of Brett Holzhauer. I traveled to Istanbul to invest in my health and appearance after a lackluster checkup at home. I flew business class round-trip using credit card rewards I'd saved for over a year. I'm pleased with the care I received and know I paid a fraction of what I would have in the US. Traveling to Turkey for medical care now has several humorous taglines and associations: men traveling for hair transplants on "Turkish Hairlines ," veneers dubbed "Turkey Teeth," and tourists walking around Istanbul looking as if they got in a back-alley brawl from post-surgery swelling. This isn't a niche market or recent trend. Millions of Americans venture internationally each year for medical or cosmetic procedures , and the market continues to grow. My interest in medical tourism began after I wrote for a travel-focused website about a viral TikTok influencer who praised the quality and affordability of medical care in Turkey. Months later, after an extremely disappointing annual physical at home in South Florida, I was compelled to seek medical care abroad. I originally planned to only get a comprehensive physical and enjoy Istanbul . After further research and some cosmetic care, I decided to indulge in a full-body reset this past April. My care was extensive The obvious overhead of participating in medical tourism is travel costs. Because the flight was roughly 10 hours, I knew I wanted to fly business class. Fortunately, I was able to save up enough credit card rewards to fly Turkish Airlines from Chicago O'Hare to Istanbul for free. The cash price of this flight is normally thousands. It was a great deal, and I used it as an excuse to see friends in Chicago for an evening before my adventure. The Memorial Hospitals Group in Turkey offers several comprehensive health checkup packages, which foreigners are able to book. I chose the most basic plan. I'm a healthy 32-year-old male, and figured I didn't need to invest more. The author was able to communicate with staff during his care through a translator who helped him in person and via WhatsApp. Courtesy of Brett Holzhauer. For $1,100 USD, I received: a full lab panel, cardiology tests, a chest X-ray, a dental radiograph, a thyroid ultrasound, and a whole-abdomen ultrasound. I also had internal medicine, ophthalmology, urology, and dental exams. Estimating an equivalent is difficult, but there are now domestic clinics , like Prenuvo, that run similar programs, though at much higher cost. I also found a cheaper dental clinic outside Memorial Hospital and got my teeth cleaned and had x-rays for only $88 USD. For cosmetic work, I had an upper and lower blepharoplasty, canthoplasty, and four moles removed. The total cost for these procedures was $6,035 USD, a fraction of what I would pay to do this near my home. The price tag included an overnight hospital stay , transportation to and from my Airbnb and the airport, two follow-up appointments, and an English-speaking translator. I did have to pay an additional $55 USD for post-surgery medications. I secured pricing months in advance, working with a hospital representative via WhatsApp. The care I received was fantastic, communication with hospital representatives was crystal clear, and I even built a friendship with my translator. During the full-body scan, she was with me the entire time. The next day, during my blepharoplasty, she was with me when I had to communicate with doctors and nurses. When I stayed overnight, the nurses knew what to do, and I didn't need to communicate with them much. But my translator was always a text away via WhatsApp, which was reassuring to me. Throughout my trip, I also opted for several massages and a haircut, all significantly cheaper than they would have been at home. My normal haircut in Florida is roughly $45, including tip; I paid $20 for a haircut, face shave, and face mask in Istanbul. Overall, I combined a two-week adventure with an investment in my health and appearance for roughly $7,500. The author said that some of his friends and family were anxious about him getting medical care abroad, but months later, he's still happy with his decision. Courtesy of Brett Holzhauer. This is the type of care I want For me, the American healthcare system doesn't offer the results it should. We spend nearly twice as much on healthcare as residents of comparable countries, yet Americans have shorter life expectancies. Despite the shortcomings of the American healthcare system, there is still a lingering fear of leaving the United States for medical care. Nearly 100 Americans died between 2009 and 2022 from cosmetic surgeries in the Dominican Republic. When I shared my plans, I could sense people's anxiety over the potential risks of getting medical care abroad. My mom offered to come with me, but I reassured her, and she ended up staying behind. Though some days were uncomfortable, and I flew home with facial bruising, the experience proved worthwhile for me. Now, months after my trip, I'm still satisfied with my results and how much I paid. For now, I'm staying put, but if I have a big medical expense in the future, I may consider going abroad again. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: ‘My hands are empty’: Displaced Palestinians struggle to survive
events.summary: Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? In the West Bank, displaced Palestinians are getting deeper into debt and living in poverty. Tulkarem, occupied West Bank – Hakim Mar’i spends his days lying on a single bed, his disfigured leg raised. The windows of Mar’i’s dilapidated apartment, his latest temporary shelter, are covered with old blankets. Unable to work, Mar’i has no money for electricity, so the blankets have to do. At night, his family lives in near darkness. The apartment is just around the corner from mounds of rubble and gnarled iron structures that mark one entrance to the now-emptied Tulkarem refugee camp. For Mar’i and other Palestinians, the camp was a home once considered temporary. But generations lived there, and now, the physical structure – their home – that tied his family together over the years is gone. list 1 of 4 UN raises ‘ethnic cleansing’ concerns over Israel’s West Bank operation list 2 of 4 Hamas slams Board of Peace for refusal to work with UNRWA in Gaza list 3 of 4 Palestine weekly: Violent disruptions from olive groves to Al-Aqsa Mosque list 4 of 4 Israeli flags become the latest weapon of settlers in West Bank domination Impoverished, Hakim’s family is in disarray. With its debts mounting and its members facing another eviction, he said he has considered taking his life several times over the past year and a half. Mar’i cannot afford treatment for his debilitating leg injury, which has developed severe infections. He said he sustained it while working as a labourer inside Israel in 2019. The wound worsened after Israeli soldiers severely beat him when they forced his family from the Tulkarem camp. Diabetes and other untreated conditions have piled on, but he is unable to pay for the needed medical care. “This joint here is completely gone,” he said, gesturing at the swollen, blackened lower leg that prevents him from working. “The medicine – by God, the medicine, I haven’t been able to get. My wife and kids tell me: get out travel. Go to America, Turkey – so I can the medical treatment I need… I’m a sick man.” His mother, Salwa, sat beside him, less than a kilometre (0.6 miles) from their former four-storey home. She wept when asked about the family home that was built floor by floor after they were first displaced in 1948 from al-Khudayra, the Arabic name for Hadera, a city in Israel. “We really put a lot into that house,” she said. After their removal, the Israeli military razed the Mar’i home so a road traversing the now-emptied camp could be built. “Seeing it destroyed was really painful for us – all of us,” she said. It has been more than 20 months since Israeli forces emptied the Jenin, Tulkarem and Nur Shams refugee camps in a sweeping military operation in the northern West Bank, displacing tens of thousands of Palestinians whose families had already been refugees for three generations. Constantly renewed orders for a closed military zone now prevent their return. Since January 2025, Hakim’s family has been forced to move four times. First, they fled to a converted youth centre before landing in a cramped apartment with their four children, all under 15. Unable to pay rent, the family could see the landlord’s generosity run its course as this once-temporary housing arrangement now has no end in sight. Hakim owes money at the local shops for food he bought on credit. Some nights, the children eat at neighbours’ houses. “I have children. I have food. I have drink,” he said. “My hands are empty. Nobody is with me. Nobody is standing beside me.” The Mar’i family is among more than 33,000 Palestinians forcibly removed from the Jenin, Nur Shams and Tulkarem camps by Israeli forces in early 2025. This is the largest single episode of forced displacement in the West Bank since Israel’s occupation began in 1967, according to the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA). UN satellite imagery shows that 20 percent of all buildings across the three camps have been destroyed and another 28 percent are damaged. “The level of destruction we are seeing is severe and unprecedented,” said Roland Friedrich, director of West Bank affairs for the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, UNRWA. According to Friedrich, 85 percent of those displaced have no regular income after many lost jobs when the camps were emptied. More than 80 percent of residents are renting, an unfamiliar expense for families who never paid for housing or utilities inside the camps. The closed military zone covering the camps is renewed every two months, Friedrich said, with no indication of when – or whether – residents will be allowed to return. “What we saw there is forced displacement,” Friedrich said. “The UN’s position is very clear: People have to be allowed to return. The camps must be rebuilt.

events.title: AI is prompting these Gen Zers to learn how to type
events.summary: Tom Vaughan-Mountford/Getty Images Gen Z grew up with phones and tablet typing, with many never learning keyboard skills. But in the age of AI-driven efficiency — and prompting — keyboard skills have a new use case. Some Gen Zers are becoming self-taught to avoid dictating AI prompts out loud. When Julia Andrusiak was in college, she noticed one of her professors repeatedly pausing his lecture. Eventually, she realized that she was the disruption: Her slow, two-finger typing was so loud that he couldn't concentrate. "It was the first moment I realized that I may not be the best at this," Andrusiak said. So she began drilling: First, she typed out books. That made her faster, but she was still staring at her keyboard. Then, she advanced to touch typing — typing without looking at the keyboard. She's still working on her speed and accuracy. Now 26, Andrusiak has an AI-focused job that involves helping people use the technology and sometimes necessitates writing strong prompts. She still can't type fast, so when she has a longer prompt, she dictates it — and feels self-conscious about what looks like talking to herself in an open office. In 2024, The Wall Street Journal reported that digital natives were baffling "teachers and parents with their lack of typing skills." Now, for some younger workers and students, typing is making a comeback . While AI might seem to harken a turn away from typing — who needs note-taking when you have an agent? — AI is only as good as the prompt it's given. Rambling voice prompts can be insufficiently clear and precise. The rise of AI has some Gen Zers looking for any efficiency edge they can carve out. "With the ever increasingly fast world, we need to type quicker. But I feel like people are really relying on AI," Andrusiak, who happily uses AI as an aid for writing and research, said. "One of my friends said, 'Well, you don't really have to type the whole page. You can just give it short sentences. It's not really that tiring.' But then I feel like it's outsourcing too much of cognitive power to a technology." Julia Andrusiak and her mechanical keyboard. Courtesy of Julia Andrusiak Typing as meditation and efficiency generator Andrey Gerasimov, a 23-year-old computer science graduate , never took typing classes. But he first needed the skill for his video game chats and decided to beef it up, eventually reaching 170 words per minute. As an AI user, he believes that faster typing makes for more efficient prompting. "You're going to be a lot more comfortable actually giving your full thoughts and ideas if you know that, hey, doing this is only going to take a minute," Gerasimov said. He's not the only one trying to up his speed and technique. In his decade teaching typing to 15 to 30-year-olds, Andreas Francazi, a 36-year-old IT teacher in Vienna, noticed that his students' typing skills have deteriorated — but they're setting out to change that. His newer crop of students didn't grow up around physical computers, and their familiarity with keyboards is much lower than previous typists. He's seen younger students come in typing rapidly with just two fingers, so he's teaching them the basics. Francazi said that students of all ages become entranced by a three-minute typing test, falling into a rapt silence. "The practice can be quite meditative," Francazi said. "You just sit there, you have the text in front of you, and you type character by character, and it kind of calms you a bit." While Francazi's screen-first students have mastered the art of two-finger typing, their future schooling and careers might necessitate the manual keyboarding skills he's teaching. Nick Sjolinder, the founder of BYOK — a purposefully distraction-free, digital typewriter device that connects to keyboards — said that around 10% of the device's orders are coming from educators, including elementary schools, middle schools, high schools, homeschools, and universities. A recent batch order came from a high school creative writing teacher, he said, with the intention of cutting down on AI and distractions for students. Tarun Krishnamurthy, an 18-year-old sophomore at San Diego State University, said his college professors speak quickly and tend to power through their slideshows. Krishnamurthi, who began intentionally practicing typing in middle school for fun, has an edge in keeping up. "I'm fortunate at least I can keep up with some of the professors, but I know some other students might have difficulty with that because they need to look at their keyboard instead of looking at the professor's slideshow," he said. And beyond fast classroom notetaking, Krishnamurthi sees his keyboard skills as a potential professional edge: In an ever-optimized and efficiency-focused world, "typing could be a big bottleneck." Slow typing could worsen workers' outputs, he said; his touch typing might give him an edge in an AI-ified world. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Ruby on Rails creator declares 'pencils down' on handwritten code
events.summary: David Heinemeier Hansson runs a software company. He's also a race car driver. Jakob Ebrey/LAT Images David Heinemeier Hansson said his software firm was "done writing code by hand." At 37signals, engineers only hand-write code when an AI agent isn't able to, Hansson said. "This is a recognition of what is already happening," he said. A coding legend is waving goodbye to handwritten code. David Heinemeier Hansson — commonly known as DHH — is the creator of the popular webapp framework Ruby on Rails. He also runs the software company 37signals, where he just instituted a new rule: "We're done writing code by hand." "We are going, and have gone, pencils down," Hansson said during the Rails World keynote. At his software company, 37signals, Hansson said that hand-writing code was an "exceptional state," only to be performed when something went wrong with the AI-generated code. When an AI agent isn't able to produce what the engineers want, they can "get the old pencil out and dot it down for them," Hansson said — but then they "fix the machine." "This is a recognition of what is already happening," he said. Indeed, coding has radically transformed in the last year, thanks to AI tools like OpenAI's Codex, Anthropic's Claude Code, and Cursor. Some developers call coding agents exhilarating, and they stay up late into the night to build with them. Others call AI coding a lonely or tiresome process . What do engineers actually think? Business Insider polled over 150 software engineers in January about the rise of vibe coding. Over 45% of respondents said they felt they were "keeping up" with AI tools. 17.5% of respondents said they were opting out of using AI code-editing tools entirely. There's only one "serious question" in this moment of coding, Hansson said at the keynote: how to best reap the rewards of AI. "Every other question is below that in the stack of values," he said. Hansson surveyed the audience: "How many people here are still writing material amounts of code by hand on a weekly basis?" After watching the crowd, Hansson let out an expletive. "That's about five," he said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: 5 BI staffers who put AI agents to work share what worked and what went wrong
events.summary: Rebecca Zisser/BI 5 BI staffers told us how they've been using the hottest new thing in AI: personal AI agents. Their use cases include reserving library books and collecting K-pop merch. One editor used it to remind him to call his mother. Muse and Instinct — AI agents designed to help you run your personal life — are the talk of the town right now. So, obviously, we at Business Insider had to try them out. Five staffers across the newsroom's global offices — from headquarters in New York to divisions in London, San Francisco, and Singapore — have been testing both Meta and Instinct's personal AI agent offerings over the past week. Our editor-in-chief, Jamie Heller, got in on the action, too: My husband and I were puzzling over an opaquely described charge on our credit card. We put the wording into Chat GPT and Muse — asking each what it could be. Chat couldn't figure it out. Muse did. Keep reading for our 101 on what worked, and what didn't . And if you have an experience of your own to share, fill out our survey . In response to our requests for comment, a Meta spokesperson pointed us to a dedicated safety post on its website. Instinct did not respond to our request for comment. Will Martin, senior editor, used Instinct to pay a car fee, but it backfired Will Martin I downloaded Instinct two weeks ago and chose a very simple task to start with: Remind me to call my mother (she worries). My whoa moment: Instinct jumped to my aid when I told it I needed a new torque wrench for my bike. After a simple prompt, Instinct came back with four options: a cheap one, a mid-priced option, and two higher-end versions — all with links and a pro/con list. In the two weeks I've been using it, Instinct has created an itinerary for a weekend trip I'm taking next year, booked tickets for my daily commute into London, and secured me a refund on an $80 subscription I forgot to cancel after the free trial. My yikes moment: This past weekend, I took a trip to Oxford, one of Britain's most notoriously complex places to drive. Oxford is famed as a warren of one-way streets, traffic cameras, and tolls. I asked my Instinct agent to pay the city's congestion charge after I drove in. Instinct obliged, cross-checking my car's model against the different emissions tiers for the charging zone, and sending me a confirmation that it had paid for two days at £4 per day. As I touted how easy it all was to my AI-skeptical partner, she pointed out that the cost was £5, not £4. So I checked, and it turned out Instinct got it wrong — it had paid a similar but separate charge for a smaller area of the city. The charge was nonrefundable, so I was forced to swallow both my own pride and an £8 tax for trusting the robots. Lesson learned, even if Instinct tried to find a silver lining. Cheryl Teh, senior news editor, used Instinct to expand her K-pop merch collection Cheryl used Instinct to formulate a targeted plan to buy K-pop albums Cheryl Teh Some people use their AI agents to save money. I decided to do the opposite and ask it to tell me how to spend my money. My whoa moment: I'm a K-pop fan, and my favorite stars — Jeonghan and Joshua, from the group Seventeen — opened preorders for their new album "Dreamscape" on Wednesday morning. I didn't have the time or energy to parse through all the listings for "preorder bonus" gifts; things like limited-run photocards and polaroids that go to fans who place their orders early. Collecting limited edition K-pop merchandise can be a bit of a blood sport , so I wanted a solid strategy. I asked Instinct to create a "buy plan" to maximize my fan experience. It took three minutes to surface a link to exclusive signed copies available for early orders on the band's US website. The agent also gave me a road map for purchase quantities and the optimal time to make those orders. Instinct saved me two hours with one prompt. Without it, I would have missed the window to purchase the US-only autographed albums. I did receive a bit of judgment from the agent — it asked me not once but twice if I'd set a cut-off budget for my buy plan. I had not, and did not intend to set one! I haven't plucked up the courage to give the agent my credit card details yet, though. My yikes moment: I was less impressed during my first 24 hours of using Instinct, when I added it to my Notion dashboard and asked it to do an overhaul. It ended up clearing out my goals calendar and schedule, and replacing it with a new — but blank — template. Instinct's WhatsApp-based chat feature is intuitive and consumer-friendly. But for optimal results, you've got to be precise in your prompts, and lay out exactly and unambiguously what you want the agent to do. Tim Paradis, future of work correspondent, put Instinct to work booking a movie ticket Instinct was helpful with some things, but also gave incorrect information. Tim Paradis The other day, I asked Instinct whether tickets were available for a 6:30 p.m. showing of "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" at a nearby theater. My whoa moment : We were on our way when Instinct texted that there wasn't a 6:30. It was 6:15, "which starts in about 8 minutes." Thank goodness for trailers — and for a speedy driver (which wasn't me). Instinct said online sales had ended, so "your only shot" was the box office. It also started checking backup films. My yikes moment : It suggested a 6:50 "Spider-Man" at another theater, but said tickets "were glitching," and gave me the theater's number. Obviously, because no one died, I wasn't going to call. The theater's site showed no "Spider-Man" that night. I told Instinct, and 16 minutes later, it said the movie "likely got pulled back." By then, we had our tickets at the original theater. "Enjoy the movie!" Instinct said. Katie Notopoulos, senior correspondent, used Muse to sign an after-school care form Katie Notopoulos My whoa moment: Most of the tasks I wanted it to do for me were related to the morass of messages and paperwork from my kids' school and activities. However, it got stuck on things like logging into the clunky school site app or being unable to check out on the Girl Scouts website. But finally, a breakthrough — I had put off the task of printing out and signing a form for after-school care. I asked Muse to fill it out for me from my email. I sent it a photo of my signature on a Post-It and used a photo of my daughter's handwritten name (she was also supposed to sign it) as her signature (morally questionable, sure). It successfully "signed" it and emailed it back to the school. My yikes moment: It offered to RSVP "no" to an invite in my email that happened to be on the same day as the Meta Connect conference. It suggested I could reply to the person and explain that this was "the most important event on my beat" — not totally wrong per se, but certainly weird to say in an email, and quite flattering to Meta. events.title: In the affordability crisis, 37% of parents are counting on financial help from the Bank of Baby Boomers and can’t wait for the Great Wealth Transfer
events.summary: Nearly two in five parents with young children, or 37%, expect to receive some sort of financial help from their own parents or grandparents over the next year, according to the BMO Real Financial Progress Index. The finding comes as the cost of raising children continues putting pressure on household budgets nationwide. BMO found that 82% of American parents say the cost of raising children has “gotten out of control,” while 86% say everyday expenses including daycare, after-school programs, summer camps and school supplies are making it harder to save for their children’s futures. Over three quarters of parents said financial support from extended family is essential to afford opportunities for their children. “Raising kids has always been a labor of love, but right now, it is also a major feat of financial engineering with families torn between spending on the urgent and the important,” BMO U.S. Head of Consumer Products Robin Growley said in the report. “Whether you are budgeting for diapers or dorm rooms, the absolute best antidote to daily financial stress is a clear, actionable plan.” And the role of the baby boomer generation isn’t just limited to writing checks. Among the parents expecting assistance, 43% depend on grandparents to provide childcare. Another 26% said family members would help fund their children’s futures through a 529 plan or another savings account. This sentiment exemplifies a shift in how American families are managing an affordability squeeze. Instead of waiting on the so-called Great Wealth Transfer, younger families are already turning to older relatives for help. According to Care.com’s 2026 Cost of Care report, parents are spending on average about 20% of their annual income on childcare—with about one in five parents spending over $30,000 a year on it. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services has identified 7% of family income as a benchmark for affordable childcare. While that’s a 2% decrease from 2025, the report found that the mental health toll increased, with about 80% spending almost every waking hour focused on someone other than themselves. And that has led to a 5% increase in parents who have considered suicide or self-harm. “Parents are being pushed well beyond their limits by the demands of caregiving,” Brad Wilson, CEO of Care.com, said in the report. “If this continues, care pressures risk pushing more parents to cut back or step away from their careers. That will only deepen financial strain and emotional stress, trapping them in a system that continues to fail them.” Housing is also a major hurdle for these families. BMO’s research found 60% of Gen Z homeowners and 57% of Millennial homeowners said they could not have purchased a home without financial support from their families. Nearly six in 10 Gen Z adults also expected to receive or ask financial help from parents or grandparents. This need for family assistance is emerging alongside a historically large concentration of wealth in older Americans. Cerulli Associates, a market research firm, estimates that $124 trillion in wealth will transfer through 2048, with nearly $100 trillion coming from baby boomers and older generations. However, that wealth won’t be evenly distributed. In Q2 2026, the top 1% of households by wealth held roughly 30% of total assets, according to Federal Reserve data, compared with about 5% held by the bottom half of households. The BMO report also found that proximity makes a difference: 45% of Americans with young children live close enough to family to receive help. Those parents reported saving an average of $1,915 a year on childcare and $1,443 on groceries compared with parents without that nearby family support. But that comes with trade-offs, with 70% of parents getting family support also being responsible for the financial or emotional well-being of their aging parents, compared to 45% of parents without family nearby. About seven in 10 parents living near relatives who provide childcare identified as being part of the “sandwich generation,” simultaneously supporting children and aging family members. “Most people make decisions to live near family with their hearts, not their spreadsheets, but those choices carry real financial consequences. Having a grandparent help raise your kids can be one of life’s greatest gifts, but family caregiving is often a reciprocal arrangement—and it can be a lot when you’re already stretched thin,” BMO’s Growley said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

Yemen’s government forces have conducted multiple air and ground operations in the southwestern governorate of Taiz in 24 hours as they intensify attacks against the Iran-backed Houthi group. The government’s military media centre on Sunday claimed several operations against the rebels, including air raids on Houthi positions in five locations across the governorate. list 1 of 4 Yemeni leader urges public to enlist, offers amnesty to Houthi defectors list 2 of 4 Yemen’s government offers amnesty to Houthi defectors list 3 of 4 The intelligence war is turning against the Houthis list 4 of 4 Why has the Yemen government called for a general mobilisation? More than 146,000 people have been displaced since the fighting erupted in July, following a period of relative calm after a United Nations-brokered ceasefire in 2022. In recent weeks, the Houthis have made dramatic territorial gains against the government forces, seizing the strategic Red Sea coastal city of Mocha and expanding their control over the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a global maritime chokepoint connecting Europe to Asia. ⁠Rashad ⁠al-Alimi, the head of the Presidential Leadership Council, has called on citizens to mobilise and join the fight against the Houthis as the government has stepped up its attacks against the Iran-backed group in an effort to stop their advance and regain lost territory. Ibrahim al-Huri, from the University of Saba in Marib governorate, said the Yemeni government’s call for a general “mobilisation” of the population will likely receive more support in the government-controlled areas, especially in Taiz and Marib, where people have been suffering more. “Even in the Houthi-controlled areas, there would be many people who would like to answer the call for mobilisation, but there will be some obstacles and challenges like the fear of retaliation and facing the brutality [of the militia].” Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia, which has faced Houthi attacks on its soil since fighting escalated this month, has been turning to its allies, including Pakistan and Turkiye, for support. Saudi Arabia backs Yemen’s internationally recognised government. Here’s what we know about the latest fighting and the humanitarian conditions the impoverished country faces: What to know about the latest fighting The military media centre said on Sunday dozens of Houthi fighters, including field commanders, were killed or wounded in the last 24 hours of fighting near Taiz’s capital, which is also named Taiz. Government forces have carried out operations in several areas of the governorate, including the al-Waziiya district in the west, weapons sites and ammunition depots at Mafraq Mawiya and al-Dhukrah in the east, a Houthi gathering in the Hayfan district in the south and against military vehicles in the Gurab area in the northwest. Government forces also thwarted infiltration attempts on the al-Ahtoub front and in Hadran as they carried out shelling of Houthi gatherings on the al-Kadha and al-Aqroud fronts, the media centre said. It added that several Houthi military vehicles were damaged in the attacks. Al Jazeera could not verify the battlefield claims. “Government forces say they have made advances in the southern Taiz governorate, taking control of several areas and higher ground. Among them is Jabal Bazel, a mountaintop that places Houthi supply lines within target range,” Al Jazeera’s Maha Ali said on Saturday, reporting from Taiz. “These developments point to significant and potentially decisive ground operations in recent hours.” Ali said al-Alimi expressed confidence that government forces were capable of restoring control over the whole country. Houthis currently control vast swaths of northern and western Yemen while the government controls the south and east. Since the current fighting erupted, the Houthis have accused the Saudis of carrying out attacks in Yemen and promised to prevent Saudi tankers from passing through Bab al-Mandeb, which Riyadh has been using as an alternative shipping route to the Strait of Hormuz amid the US-Israel war on Iran. Tehran has effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz since the United States and Israel began the war in February. Before the conflict, a fifth of the world’s oil supplies had passed through Hormuz. Government forces, meanwhile, accused the Houthis of using Iranian air defence weapons and said they pose a danger to aircraft. “These Houthi weapons pose a serious threat to international flight paths over the Red Sea and operate using a heat-tracking system,” Brigadier-General Majed al-Nazili, the Yemeni government forces’ spokesperson, said on social media. “The weapons employed are capable of attacking military or civilian targets without the ability to distinguish between them, thereby endangering the safety of civil aviation and the lives of passengers.

events.title: The startup trap that kept this longevity app founder stuck
events.summary: Brent Franson is the CEO of Death Clock. Courtesy of Death Clock Death Clock CEO Brent Franson said startups can get stuck in a phase he calls "slow failure." He shut down his startup and threw out years' worth of code to build Death Clock, a consumer-health product. When a startup isn't viable , Franson says, founders should fully pivot rather than try to patch it. Brent Franson spent four years building a mental-health app that users liked, but that didn't ultimately work as a business. The product wasn't an obvious flop. It had enough promise, he said, to make further rounds of changes seem worthwhile — the trap of something that seemed "pretty good," though ultimately isn't viable. "Mediocrity is so dangerous," Franson said. In late 2024, seeing a need for a fresh start, he shut down the app, called Most Days, and discarded the codebase that his team had spent years building. The San Francisco-based staff then shifted their attention to building a consumer-health product called Death Clock, which Franson, 44, described as an "AI private doctor." Users enter health information — ranging from cholesterol levels to diet and sleep habits — and the platform uses longevity research to estimate the age at which they might die and suggest changes that could help them live longer. The experience reshaped how the longtime early-stage entrepreneur, who in 2019 sold a prior software company he ran to WeWork, thinks about startups. Here are three lessons Franson has learned: An app people like is not necessarily a viable business Most Days had users, though the company could not acquire them cheaply enough to build a sound business, he said. The scary part of pivoting , Franson said, is not when a business is clearly failing or obviously taking off. It is when a product has users who like it and just enough promise to make another round of changes seem worthwhile. "You can convince yourself to keep iterating on it," he said. Franson, who is CEO of Death Clock, calls that danger "slow failure": a business that lingers because its leaders keep rationalizing why it might soon work. One test, he said, is whether founders are working through concrete problems with conviction or trying to talk themselves into continuing. When you pivot, make a clean break For Franson, the response wasn't to rebrand Most Days or look for another half-measure like a savvy hire. It was to shut it down completely. He said the hardest decision was abandoning a company the team had spent years building and still believed served an important mental-health need. Yet, Franson said, the team concluded that they needed to make a clean break and a full bet on Death Clock. The team carried no code from Most Days over to their new venture, Franson said. The decision also meant embracing a name he initially saw as a potentially terrible mistake. The team had considered calling the product "More Years," Franson said, before deciding to keep the more provocative working name they had been using internally. A good product needs a way to reach customers Franson said the failure of Most Days taught him that product quality alone wouldn't cut it. A consumer company also needed a way to get attention without spending heavily to buy it, he said. When Franson went to Most Days' investors about the shift, he said they faced a choice: Take back a fraction of their investment or support the Death Clock idea. Their reactions to the name were sharply divided, Franson said. "People either loved the name Death Clock, or they hated it, but they didn't forget it," he said. Franson came to see the name as a distribution strategy in a crowded consumer-health market, where companies with ample funding can spend heavily to acquire customers. Death Clock's name comes with risks, he said, including whether the attention-grabbing approach will keep people from taking it seriously as a consumer-health product. The episode reinforced an idea that Franson now cites about building startups : First-time founders focus on product; second-time founders focus on distribution. While the company's name is provocative , Franson said the company remains restrained about the health interventions it recommends. Death Clock doesn't sell peptides , he said, because the company's clinical advisors don't believe the science supports their use. It's a choice that means forgoing potential revenue, Franson said. The lesson he took from Most Days was not that founders should never persist, but that they should recognize when it has become a form of rationalization. "It's hard to tell the difference, a lot of times, between slow success and slow failure," he said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: This small town librarian offers a 'Bye, Bye AI' class to take AI off your phone. Now everyone wants in.
events.summary: Shea Wert, library director of the North Chatham Free Library, will be holding a "Bye Bye AI" event to help people turn off AI features on their phones. Shea Wert A small upstate New York library is offering a "Bye Bye AI" event. The librarian will help people turn off AI features on their phones or email. She told BI she's also happy to help people set up AI. The event has gone viral, with people around the world wanting to tune in. North Chatham, a hamlet in upstate New York halfway between Hudson and Albany, doesn't have much going on. You have to go to the next hamlet over for a store or restaurant. There's a church, a post office, and a small public library with only about 800 cardholders. The North Chatham Free Library has gotten a lot of attention lately, however, after a flyer for an upcoming "Bye Bye AI" event offering to remove the AI features from your phone or laptop went viral on Facebook, getting over 200 comments and 8,000 likes. The poster was made by the library's sole full-time librarian, Shea Wert. Wert told Business Insider that she had made this event in response to community demand — and was surprised by the reaction from far-flung places. "Do I live anywhere near this library? No. Am I in support of this? Hell yeah!" wrote one commenter. The event flyer went viral on Facebook, getting comments from around the world. https://www.facebook.com/share/p/1J7QUQUcU2/ "I had to look at the library's main page to see where Chatham is. I'm in central CA and wonder if we can have a digital guide that our own Mariposa County Library could use for a similar program?" wrote another. "As someone in Ohio who just happened upon this post; will this be streamed or recorded?" someone else asked. "As somewhere near Chatham, UK, I was a little confused at first Regardless, thanks Shea!" a jolly Brit wrote. The library does weekly tech support drop-in hours, and in April it held an "AI for seniors" class that covered the basics of AI and LLMs. But this latest offering was something new. The idea was based on requests Wert had noticed from the community. "There's just been enough patrons asking about certain things that bothered them, specifically Gmail auto replies and auto completes really frustrate people," Wert told Business Insider during a recent phone call. "I went to a presentation that another librarian was doing about this topic, and they had had success with it. And I was like, 'Okay, well, I've heard enough from my patrons that they're worried about this stuff or frustrated about this stuff that I might as well try to do one.'" The library held an "AI for seniors" class earlier this year that covered the basics. North Chatham Free Library That other librarian, Hannah Cyrus, published a column in a journal of library studies, writing that "libraries have a role to play in facilitating patrons' rejection of technology, just as much as in their adoption of it." Cyrus has offered a series of free classes for patrons, teaching them how to turn off or avoid AI tools on their phones and computers, with great success — and a much larger turnout than other tech classes. TechCrunch reported in July that Cyrus's article in the library journal inspired other librarians to reach out and ask for help running their own versions of the classes. "I've heard from hundreds of librarians from all over the world asking for my presentation slides," she told Business Insider. The North Chatham Free Library serves a tiny hamlet in upstate New York, with only about 800 library card holders. Shea Wert One of the groups that reached out was a consortium of libraries for the Hudson Valley area, which included the North Chatham Free Library. Cyrus gave a webinar to a group of librarians, including Wert, about how she ran the "Avoiding AI" class. In Wert's personal life, she admits to staying a bit of a Luddite, preferring to use a dumbphone . But she's not adamantly anti-AI and has used AI tools for work to draft outlines or write dense policy text. "There have been some patrons that I know are using LLMs, and I'm happy to help them with it. I've helped them write better prompts, although that is far less common," she said. "It's more common that they haven't used it and they don't want to use it." Both Wert and Cyrus said that most of the people who come in for help with AI or tech in general are older adults, who are often frustrated by new AI features on the services they already use. The Bye-Bye AI event will take place next week, and Wert isn't entirely sure what to expect given the viral reaction on Facebook. "I'm a little concerned based on setting it up as a drop-in thing that there'll be people waiting because I can only help so many at one time," she said. "But I don't know. If 20 people come, that would feel like a lot to me." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: With no heirs to leave it to, this billionaire is pouring his fortune into a Texas ghost town of about 25 people
events.summary: The $124 trillion Great Wealth Transfer is underway , and baby boomers are passing down their fortunes to their heirs.  But what happens when an ultrawealthy person has no descendants? In the case of 81-year-old billionaire John Poindexter , he’s getting creative and funneling some of his wealth into a quite unexpected cause: a super small town in West Texas.  Shafter, Texas, is a ghost town in a county that just keeps getting emptier. Presidio County had an estimated 5,433 residents in 2025, down 11.4% since 2020 and down from 7,818 in 2010, Census Bureau data shows. The median household income is just $43,802 (about half the median U.S. income ), nearly one in five residents lives in poverty, and only about 1.6 people live per square mile. But Poindexter, a Houston manufacturing magnate, is betting on it anyway. Since late 2020, his Tidewater and Big Bend Foundation has taken in nearly $67 million in contributions, according to IRS filings compiled by ProPublica . That includes $20.6 million in the fiscal year ending November 2024, when the foundation reported $62.5 million in net assets. The foundation’s signature project is Shafter, the former silver-mining town where about 25 people live, according to the Big Bend Sentinel . The plans, according to the Times , call for a resort and living history museum anchored by a rebuilt saloon, general store, and post office, with about a dozen adobe homes available for overnight rentals. When the Times asked why his family won’t inherit his wealth instead, Poindexter said: “I’ve never been married, I have no children.” That’s a different path from Warren Buffett, who has directed his $140 billion wealth to four of his family’s foundations so they can choose how to spend it. With no children to hand the reins to, Poindexter is building his own. Poindexter’s foundation will eventually own all of his properties, the Times reported, including the 30,000-acre Cibolo Creek Ranch where Justice Antonin Scalia died in 2016 . ‘The place is going to boom’ Shafter’s Presidio Mine operated from 1883 to 1942 and produced 35.2 million ounces of silver, according to Black Bear Minerals , which now owns it. After the mine closed, the town emptied out. By early 2025, Poindexter had bought several Shafter properties and offered to restore the historic church at the town’s entrance, the Big Bend Sentinel reported. Not every resident is sold on the plan, but a new restaurant and shop would likely be welcome. For now, the closest place to buy groceries is Presidio, which is 19 miles away. Shafter resident and water board president David Long told the Sentinel the preservation efforts could spur more people to move to the ghost town. “This is a wake-up call for sure, for people to start considering what’s going to happen to the town,” Long told the Sentinel . “Once we get a dependable, good water system in here, the place is going to boom.” How Poindexter made his fortune and dedicated it to restoration Poindexter served in Vietnam, received two Silver Stars and two Purple Hearts, and spent 14 years in finance before founding J.B. Poindexter & Co. in 1985. He remains its sole owner. While his net worth isn’t public, the Times characterized him as a billionaire.  His company grew from $40 million in revenue in 1994 to more than $2.7 billion in annualized revenue through more than 40 acquisitions, according to a 2024 EY announcement naming him a regional Entrepreneur of the Year. The company builds the bodies of UPS’s brown delivery trucks and says it produces 66% of the step vans in the U.S. class five delivery market.  Poindexter isn’t the first rich American to try to restore a town’s past. The Shafter plan is “kind of the same as Colonial Williamsburg, where you can actually stay in town and then some of the structures will just be museum visiting,” Henry Thompson, an officer of Poindexter’s foundation, told the Big Bend Sentinel . The Colonial Williamsburg restoration dates back to 1926, when John D. Rockefeller Jr. began quietly buying up properties in the former Virginia capital, according to the Colonial Williamsburg Foundation . He insisted on staying anonymous, and a year later he committed $5 million to restore the whole town. Not everyone was on board. When the Rockefellers were finally revealed as the donors at a town meeting, at least one resident stood up to object . Poindexter, meanwhile, is taking a much more public approach. He invited about 200 guests to Shafter over Labor Day weekend, the Times reported.  It’s also a different bet from the ones today’s tech billionaires are making. A group of Silicon Valley investors spent roughly $800 million buying up Solano County farmland to build California Forever, an entirely new city, and faced plenty of local backlash along the way. In other words, they want to build the future from scratch. Poindexter wants to bring back the past. “I think that we’ve forgotten our origins,” he told the Times . “We’ve forgotten this enormous debt we have to prior generations.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Big AI's content problem: Take the work, keep the money
events.summary: Big AI has a problem. Its companies must ingest other people’s work. You know, books, news stories, photographs, code, websites, that one original meme you came up with, and practically everything else on the internet to train its large language models (LLMs). We all know that. We also know that AI companies hate paying for any of it, obeying the licenses attached to it, or, God forbid, sharing their revenue with the companies and people who created the work in the first place. Recently, Big AI's default way of doing business: "Take it now, argue about legality later," has become more in your face than ever. Look, for example, at the copyright fight between The New York Times and OpenAI and Microsoft. According to 404 Media’s reporting on recently unsealed court documents - arguments from the plaintiffs that the court has not yet ruled on - Microsoft allegedly knew what it was doing when it was importing the internet willy-nilly. Microsoft's Director of Applied Science, Dr. Brent Hecht, was quoted in the news plaintiffs' 92-page combined brief as saying: the case was about “an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions." Indeed, it was possibly the “largest theft of labor in human history,” he was quoted as saying in the summary judgment brief from the journalists' lawyers [PDF].This, mind you, wasn't a comment by a member of the press; it was from a senior Microsoft staffer. Hecht wasn't the only one at Microsoft who commented. In an internal Microsoft policy document also quoted in the court papers, the authors admitted generative AI could “significantly disrupt the employment of the very people who generated the data on which the foundation model was trained [because] LLMs are a product that destroys its supply chain.” That, in turn, leads to model collapse. Ironically, AI is killing the content-creator goose that lays the gold eggs of worthwhile content. Judge Sidney H. Stein of the US District Court for the Southern District of New York has not yet issued a decision on the case. OpenAI and Microsoft are actively disputing the plaintiffs' allegations under a "fair use" defense. They contend that using public articles and books to train large language models helps push forward public knowledge, and isn't acting as a "unlawful economic market substitute". But the statements the documents cites are real. Big AI knows it needs the content. Some of the companies concerned don't give a damn; money now, worry later is their motto. Those who can look past the revenue numbers are well aware they're engaged in what Microsoft itself called a “doom loop” of AI content strategy in those unsealed court documents. Will that stop them? Nah. According to the filing [PDF], which refers to sworn deposition testimony of OpenAI’s own corporate representative, it also testified that its LLMs were happy to vacuum up other people's work even when a paywall nominally protected it. Its rep was quoted as saying they were unaware of “any effort to detect paywall content in its training datasets” or “to remove paywall content from its training datasets.” When OpenAI cofounder Greg Brockman was told OpenAI could hack its way through the firewall, he responded, “ah, nice.” Whether or not these statements are found to be reflective of a wider attitude, similar attitudes prevail amongst Big AI. Such policies could eventually come back and bite the LLM makers; it's already affecting the market for journalism, fiction writing, graphics creation, anything that demands humans actually get paid for producing original work. But Big AI just doesn't want to pay for it. That's not a side effect. It's the business model. Joe User couldn't care less. They just want a quick answer that sounds right. Some of them couldn't care less about getting the right answers. As for looking deeper to see if the information they're regurgitating is accurate, forget about it! As an OpenAI software engineer put it: “No matter how prominently we show the links, users won’t click.” Well, I click. That's a big reason why Perplexity is my AI of choice. It's not that it gives a more reliable answer. No, it's that, unlike most LLMs, Perplexity provides sources and links, and I check them before accepting what it tells me. But then I'm a journalist whose degrees are in history, where my professors drummed into me that you always - always - look at the primary sources. Big AI takes the same approach with its code generators. The US Ninth Circuit recently handed GitHub, Microsoft, and OpenAI a narrow win in the Doe v. GitHub lawsuit. The court ruled that the plaintiffs hadn't established a claim under one particular provision of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA), which concerns the removal or alteration of copyright-management information (CMI). In short, the court said that generating new code without including CMI is not necessarily the same thing as removing or altering copyright information from an existing work. Judge Eric Miller wrote: “One who creates a new work and fails to include CMI cannot be said to have ‘removed’ or ‘altered’ anything.” This ruling didn't establish that GitHub Copilot or any other coding model may train on every open source project without restriction. It didn't determine that copying source code into a training set is always fair use. It did not decide that generated code cannot infringe copyright. And it certainly did not repeal the GPL, Apache, BSD, MIT, or any other open-source license. After all, open source isn't a synonym for “do whatever you want with it.” It just seems that way when AI gets its hands on open source code. That's the problem with AI-generated code. A programmer who receives a Copilot suggestion is very unlikely to check whether the GPL covers the code, or whether Apache covers the snippet from a library. The developer certainly can't tell which license terms may apply to the code that just popped up from Opus 5.5 or GPT 6. As the guy from OpenAI said, people don't click the links, and in AI-enabled programming pipelines, they don't even have the links anyway. An open source-savvy attorney friend of mine has a bigger worry than this narrow decision. He told me that what gives him "pause is a broader trend. There are multiple cases where parties are litigating open source licenses as contracts rather than as the IP / copyright licenses they were written to be. Contract theories let a plaintiff sidestep the questions copyright forces you to answer. 'Do you own the work? Is it protectable expression? Was it actually copied?'" He added: "Those questions are the foundation on which licenses are built. Open source licenses are grants of permission to use someone's intellectual property. If a case can't show that any intellectual property was owned or infringed, it's fair to ask whether enforcing the license as a bare contract supports open source licensing or quietly turns it into something else." events.title: David Rubenstein shares his recipe for career success — and says boomers like him 'don't want to get off the stage'
events.summary: David Rubenstein is the billionaire cofounder of Carlyle. Bloomberg/Getty Images David Rubenstein says reading, writing, speaking, and passion will serve young people in the AI era. The billionaire told Business Insider he swore off gambling at age 16 and won't retire anytime soon. The Baltimore Orioles owner just released a book featuring his interviews with other team owners. AI may be transforming the world of work , but the core ingredients for a successful career haven't changed, David Rubenstein says. "For a young person, the best thing to do is: Learn how to read and enjoy reading, learn how to speak effectively and persuasively , and learn how to write reasonably well," the billionaire investor told Business Insider in a recent, wide-ranging interview. The cofounder of private equity giant Carlyle also said to "find something that you really enjoy and make it your life's work." "If you really enjoy something, it's not work, and you'll do much better at it ," he continued. "Nobody ever won a Nobel Prize hating what they do." Rubenstein, 77, acknowledged that more and more people are relying on AI chatbots to read and write, but he said the ability to discern between good and bad writing will remain important. "I just think the basic skills that have gotten people to be successful over the last several thousand years are probably not going to go away ," he said. Rubenstein spoke to BI ahead of the release of his latest book this week: "Inside the Owner's Box: Conversations on Power and Leadership in Sports." Recipe for success The principal owner of the Baltimore Orioles baseball team also shared insights from his personal life. Rubenstein said that as a wealthy parent, he kept his children grounded by emphasizing the value of education and work ethic to them, and "tried to be a role model by showing how hard work can lead to something productive." All three of his kids went on to secure MBAs from Harvard or Stanford, and now work in private equity, he said. But he underscored that regardless of parents' best efforts, there's no guarantee how their children will turn out. Asked about work-life balance, Rubenstein said he doesn't view his work as a "chore" or "drudgery," and feels " fortunate that I can do things I really want to do." In recent years, he's pivoted from investing to interviewing everyone from Warren Buffett and Jamie Dimon to Bill and Hillary Clinton, while also publishing seven books and counting. Rubenstein said that owning a sports team has improved his work-life balance "because you have to go to games if you're going to be an effective owner , and I didn't go to that many games before." The Wall Street veteran also touched on sports betting, saying that after he lost $18 on a bet in high school, he swore off gambling for life. "I learned my lesson when I was 16," he said. Rubenstein said that if sports betting were to go away, "it wouldn't upset me, but I think it's here to stay." He also discussed the trend of baby boomers working later in life. He and a lot of his friends are working as hard in their mid-70s as they were 10 or 20 years earlier, he said, as "we don't want to get off the stage ." Rubenstein said he doesn't know what he'd do with himself if he retired, and he worries there's a greater risk of dropping dead after retirement. "So I'm not retiring anytime soon ," he said. events.title: A former BCG partner says leaving consulting taught him how to build
events.summary: Daniel Dantus is a former BCG consultant who pivoted into tech. CMAND Daniel Dantus spent over eight years at BCG after graduating from the University of Michigan in 2011. He later moved to Juul and now works at Skan AI, a platform for observing AI agent behavior. "If a job does not work out the way you thought, you can always get another one"," he says This is an as-told-to conversation with Daniel Dantus, a former BCG partner who's now a senior vice president at Skan AI, a startup that analyzes how work happens across a company. This conversation has been condensed and edited for clarity. I came into consulting as an undergraduate at the University of Michigan's business school. I joined a student consulting club and landed at Boston Consulting Group in Chicago, first as an intern, and then full time. What was special about BCG was that you were given a lot of rope from day one. My first week was training. By the second, I was on a manufacturing floor working with a large food-and-beverage company. We flew to Dallas and Mexico and visited plants. I was 20 years old. I was learning to enter new environments, build relationships, and have an impact. I was at BCG for a total of eight years. For the first six, every project involved a different client, city, and team. Firms recommend continuity, but I loved diving into new things. I did operations work in manufacturing and supply chain, as well as in financial services. Later, after I moved to San Francisco, I worked in tech, focusing on sales and product strategy. When I was promoted to project leader, my work shifted from delivering work to figuring out where I was going to build a business. I realized I wanted to keep learning and building products, which consulting projects generally do not allow over the long term. So I took some transition time from the firm, which is paid time to take a breather and find the next thing. I made a list of companies I thought might be interesting and people I knew who might be worth talking to. I had about 100 conversations. Job searches are a numbers game, like sales. If you want to sell to 10 customers, you'd better start talking to 200. That process led me to Harbor Freight Tools, a tool and equipment retailer, as the Director of Marketing, right after BCG. The mandate was to build out the company's digital marketing capability. It was my first "real job" after consulting, and I wasn't sure how learning to build PowerPoints would translate into delivering results. Still, by launching and scaling HFT's digital marketing channels across search, social, and display, I learned it did. Two years later, I ended up at Juul. I had worked with the head of corporate strategy on a BCG project when he worked at Constellation Brands. He later went to Juul to build a new capability. I reached out to catch up, and it happened to be good timing. I started working on its corporate strategy team, then later ran global travel retail and product. It was a turbulent time for the company. We went from about 1,000 employees to about 4,000 and then back to 1,000. It was also the first time I got to run a business over a longer term. Travel retail was my first sales job. You learn what it is like to be told no, to negotiate hard, to develop relationships, and to stand your ground. In my final two years, I ran product and e-liquid development, my first technical role alongside a business role. I learned how to take a product to market. I later returned to BCG as a partner. My work consisted of serving private equity clients in strategic due diligence. My advice to people leaving consulting is that no single job is that important. Take time to pause and reflect, and do outreach in addition to considering inbound opportunities. If a job does not work out the way you thought, you can always get another one. I joined Skan last year after reconnecting with its founders. It's a surprising turn of events. Five years earlier, I thought the problem the company was trying to solve was impossible: How do you use passive observation to understand a complex workflow, such as an insurance claim that takes two months to resolve? Generative AI has made it easier to automate work where existing data — documents, databases, calls, and chats — is available. There's still a gap between clicks and tacit knowledge that explains how to execute a business process, and it's one of the biggest opportunities in enterprise AI. After over a year at Skan, I know one thing: AI is just accelerating the same hard work that has always needed to be done. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Malaysia’s Ng, Subramaniam book LA28 Olympics berth with Asian Games gold
events.summary: The top seeds defend their Asian Games squash titles, becoming the first players to qualify for the Los Angeles Games. Malaysia’s Eain Yow Ng and Sivasangari Subramaniam have made history by becoming the first squash players to qualify for the 2028 Olympics after winning gold medals at the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan. The defending champions won the men’s and women’s singles finals on Sunday and earned a ticket to the 2028 Los Angeles Games, where squash will make its Olympic debut. list 1 of 4 Yuki Kurihara, Japan’s 11-year-old e-sports prodigy, wins Asian Games gold list 2 of 4 N Korea’s Ri breaks three weightlifting records, India’s Chanu bags silver list 3 of 4 ‘It’s our time to shine’: India’s surfers look to make waves at Asian Games list 4 of 4 Japan’s Ohashi breaks 200m breaststroke world record at Asian Games Squash is among a handful of sports at Aichi-Nagoya where a gold medal serves as automatic qualification for the next Olympics. Both Ng and Subramaniam successfully defended their titles without dropping a single game in their campaigns. Their victories gave Malaysia its fifth and sixth gold medals. World number 18 Ng thrashed India’s Abhay Singh 11-9, 11-5, 11-5 in 33 minutes at the Nagoya Kinjo Futo Arena and became the first Malaysian to qualify for the Olympics. World number five Subramaniam joined her compatriot soon after when she made quick work of the women’s final against India’s Anahat Singh. She demolished Singh, ranked 17th in the world, 11-4, 11-4, 11-7 in just 23 minutes to clinch gold. Earlier, Singh, the world junior champion, produced a stellar comeback in the semifinals from two sets down to overpower Japan’s Satomi Watanabe (9-11, 11-13, 12-10, 11-6, 11-3) on Saturday. “I think it is the best win of my career,” Singh, 18, said after the match. “She’s number six in the world, and that’s the highest win I’ve ever had in my squash career.” She made history even before Sunday’s match began when her semifinal victory made her the first Indian woman to reach the singles final at the Asian Games. Earlier in the day, Pakistan picked up two more bronze medals at the games as third seed Noor Zaman toppled compatriot Ashab Irfan 3-0 in the bronze medal match. Watanabe took a 3-1 win over Hong Kong’s Sin Yuk Chan.

events.title: They couldn't afford nursing homes for their parents. They built them a tiny home instead.
events.summary: Jimmy Barton lives in a tiny home purchased by Justin Barton and daughter-in-law Linda Barton. Joseph Bui for BI ADUs are popular for multigenerational living, offering affordable alternatives to nursing homes. Building ADUs can be complex and costly, but they provide family support and community proximity. "Having everyone on the same property is enormously valuable," one source told Business Insider. Over the last few years, Linda Barton watched as her mom and stepdad progressively shifted from active 80-year-olds to, in her words, "children." Her mom with dementia became unable to take care of herself, while her stepfather, whose health has also declined, "acts like he's 6 years old." The commute to see them, which was an hour each way from work, wore her down, and she didn't want them to move in with her because of space constraints. She did the next best thing: move them into her yard. Linda Barton and her husband bought two tiny homes for their three living parents. Joseph Bui for BI Barton, 55, and her husband bought a tiny home for $37,000 in their part of Texas, outside Houston. After months of installing a septic system, an electrical line, an entrance ramp, and indoor essentials, her parents moved in. A year later, they purchased another tiny home for her father-in-law on their property for $43,000. They've hired caregivers for their three parents at rates below assisted living, making caregiving more manageable. Still, it's not a perfect solution. Barton said she's "drowning" in caregiving bills because neither Medicare nor hospice has provided much financial relief. Linda Barton said the arrangement has worked well for her and her parents. Joseph Bui for BI "If we don't pay for caregivers, we end up sacrificing work when they need something," Barton said. "It's exhausting, and we fear we won't live to see our own retirement due to the stress." Caregiving costs have skyrocketed in recent years. Instead of emptying their wallets to pay for pricy rooms in nursing homes, Americans like Barton are building tiny houses, renovating sheds, and buying trailers as housing options for their aging loved ones who need full-time care. Are you paying for your own or your loved one's long-term care? Do you have thoughts to share about long-term care in the US? To share your story with a reporter, please fill out this quick form . With construction costs typically ranging from $100,000 to $300,000, not including expenses such as hiring an architect, setting up utilities, or obtaining construction permits, these accessory dwelling units require a significant investment. But the cost of even one year in a nursing home can be comparable: The service and insurance company CareScout found that annual private room costs in nursing homes rose from $111,000 to $130,000 between 2022 and 2025. ADUs for caregiving have boomed in popularity When Shalini Karnani Bonjour's father died in 2024, she moved her aging mother from Michigan to California to be closer to her family. At first, Bonjour, 50, considered renting an apartment for her mother or moving her into a senior-living community , but neither option was ideal. Instead, Bonjour's family bought a home in the Coachella Valley with plans to build an ADU in the backyard where her mother can live independently. The $475,000 project is pricey, but more affordable than buying a larger home in the area. Although it was the family's best option, Bonjour, 50, said, "The whole process has been difficult because there are so many things to manage. You're trying to keep the project affordable, keep your neighbors happy, and stay on track." ADUs have become increasingly popular in California, attracting the attention of politicians and housing advocates to ease the state's housing crisis. Rachael Reiner, director of pre-construction and project management at the Bay Area-based ADU company Villa , told Business Insider that ADUs have become especially popular among multigenerational households . 75% of Villa's sales so far in 2026 have been for that purpose, many for caregiving purposes. "The California housing market is so competitive and expensive, so for many families, finding a larger home or a second home within budget simply isn't realistic," Reiner said. "Building an ADU on an existing family property can allow these families to stay rooted in a neighborhood that they already know, without changing schools or their routines — especially for an aging family member, a routine can be so important." An emotional decision Linda Barton has played the role of caregiver while having some separation. Joseph Bui for BI Sometimes, the decision to build an ADU to care for a loved one is driven by emotional rather than financial factors. Lena Koropey decided to build an ADU in her Long Island backyard to allow her mother, who has later-stage Alzheimer's, to age in place. Once the two-bedroom, one-bathroom, 750-square-foot home is completed, the plan is for Koropey to move into the backyard so her mother and her full-time live-in caregiver can stay in the main house. The plan isn't cheap — a full-time live-in caregiver from the firm she hired costs between $520 and $550 per day, and her ADU is estimated at about $450,000 — but Koropey said it will be worth it. "Having everyone on the same property is enormously valuable," Koropey, 48, told Business Insider. "You can't really put a price on that sense of community, the bond of family, or the ability to support one another." Despite the cost cutting from these " granny flats ," most of the over a dozen people Business Insider interviewed said navigating the permitting process was a hassle. Some mentioned burdensome costs they hadn't anticipated. A few were wary of installing an ADU for fear of reducing their property value, while others regretted it after their loved ones moved out shortly thereafter. "ADUs are helpful for certain situations where the care need isn't that great, or where somebody in the house has time to provide that greater care," Mildred Warner, a professor of city and regional planning at Cornell University who has studied ADUs, said. "There are other situations where it makes more sense to have people in older-adult apartment complexes." James Richard Cornell built his mom a house from scratch. Cornell Watson for BI Some families told Business Insider that because the ADU permitting process was so complex, they decided to build a house on a separate property. After nearly a year of trying to build an ADU, James Richard Cornell, 63, decided to build his mom a house on his property from scratch. Between 2013 and 2014, he obtained a permit, cleared the foundation, and installed plumbing, flooring, and siding. The 1,000-square-foot home cost about $110,000, and his mom paid for 90% of it. His mom has since moved into his main home following a vascular dementia diagnosis .
