events.title: My husband and I work full-time but had to borrow money to pay for my dad's cremation
events.summary: Heather Waughtel's father died in 2026. Courtesy of Heather Waughtel When Heather Waughtel's dad died, a family friend covered the cremation after her card was declined. Waughtel and her husband both work full-time, but live paycheck to paycheck. "We're barely making enough to live. How can we afford for someone to die?" she said. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Heather Waughtel, 47, a project coordinator based in Knoxville, Tennessee. Business Insider has verified her income and her dad's funeral costs. It has been edited for length and clarity. Before my dad died, I felt we had been responsible by discussing things like finances and the power of attorney. Dad had life insurance and said the cremation would be covered. I soon learned that when a loved one dies in the US, you must deal with financial and legal questions while in the rawest stage of grief. Did you take on debt or make major financial sacrifices after losing a loved one? Business Insider would like to hear from you for a series about the cost of dying. Please fill out this quick form. Dad died in July, at age 71. About two days later, a family friend and I called credit card companies, insurers, and the bank to close out Dad's accounts. That was how we discovered the life insurance policy had been cashed out. There was also no inheritance : Dad's estate was small and insolvent, with some credit card debt. My husband and I both work full-time — I'm a project coordinator and he's a painter for a boat repair shop — but we still live paycheck to paycheck and our finances are always a concern. Sometimes, we have to choose between buying food and gas to get to work. We had no way to pay for Dad's cremation, so a family friend loaned us the money. I didn't feel I had any other choice. My dad died sooner than we expected In the early 2000s, Dad transitioned and began identifying as a woman. She thought everyone would be upset, but I respected her so much for coming out and being open and honest about who she was. It was a major, positive turning point in our relationship after years of estrangement, and we remained close until the end of her life. Heather Waughtel's dad, who transitioned in the early 2000s, had a lung condition in her final years. Courtesy of Heather Waughtel Her death didn't come as a total surprise, although it happened a little sooner than we expected. In the final years of her life, she had COPD and a chronic lung infection, and often struggled to breathe. In early June, she went into a nursing home as her health deteriorated, and she rapidly declined. A month and a bit later, she was gone. I thought we were prepared for Dad's death I thought there would be some money to cover the immediate costs of her death, such as the cremation, but Dad had cashed out her life insurance policy a week before she died. I still don't know why. The funeral package, which included transferring her from the nursing home to the funeral home, her cremation, the container for her ashes, service, and death certificates, cost around $3,700. The family friend went with me to the funeral home to arrange Dad's cremation, and my credit card was declined. She put the charge on hers without me asking. I felt guilty and kept thinking I should have used the power of attorney to make sure everything was taken care of before she died. Heather Waughtel, right, with her dad, Cathy. Courtesy of Heather Waughtel I could have gotten a second job to pay the friend back, but I already work 7:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., then drive home. Crowdfunding felt like my only option. I felt defeated. I find myself anxious to take the site down, but I have to talk myself out of it. There is embarrassment in asking people to help pay a bill that should have been taken care of. There is embarrassment in not having the money. It has been hard to grieve while in debt Since all this happened, my husband and I attended a wills and trusts seminar . I've reviewed my life insurance policies and made sure everything is in order. I'm determined that my four adult children will not be left with a mess like this. I still haven't scattered Dad's ashes. I haven't felt comfortable while the anxiety over paying the money back hangs over me. This situation has left me agitated. It has been hard to process my grief. The system feels broken: too commercial, too American, and I hate that there are people making money off people dying. We're barely making enough to live. events.title: Bill Gates says unchecked AI could ‘cause a billion deaths’ in call for regulation
events.summary: Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist speaks with NBC’s Kristen Welker in interview airing on Sunday Bill Gates has called on the US’s federal legislators and law enforcers to regulate the development of artificial intelligence (AI), saying in an interview airing on Sunday that the technology left unchecked could cause “a billion deaths” and “no one thinks self-regulation is enough”. “You need law enforcement and the politicians to get into the discussion about what safeguards and monitoring look like,” the Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist said to Kristen Welker, the NBC Meet the Press host. “And that has to be a required thing.” Using a term meant to describe an expense required to run a business, Gates continued: “It will be a little bit of overhead for the industry – but not a dramatic slowing of what they’re doing.” Another portion of the interview – excerpts of which NBC circulated in advance – saw Gates dramatically admonish that AI in the wrong hands would be “certainly powerful enough to drive events that, you know, cause a billion deaths”. “There’s never been a weapon as powerful as the combination of people with ill intent using the latest AI tools,” Gates added, echoing other recent similar warnings by a wide array of tech and political figures. Gates otherwise is generally regarded as optimistic about humans’ future. Many reporting or commenting on his conversation with Welker noted that it occurred in the wake of a nearly 6,000-word essay that he published in late August warning about AI and the potentially lethal ills it poses to humanity on a large scale. His fellow tech moguls including Sam Altman and Elon Musk have joined Gates in calling for a slowdown of the development of AI, which some experts theorize could precipitate the mass destruction of humans through bioweapons and nuclear war, among other methods. Meanwhile, Microsoft itself has been challenged for having a role in stoking some of the dystopian concerns surrounding AI. Company employees and activists have organized a campaign aimed at getting Microsoft to cut ties with the Israeli military, which has used AI tools to kill in Gaza and – alongside US forces – in Iran, according to a Guardian essay published on Friday. The essay’s authors, Mohamed Hussein and Granate Kim of the No Azure for Apartheid group, furthermore warned that “horrors wrought by AI” are also being seen in the US. For instance, the US Department of Homeland Security has used AI tools such as Microsoft’s Azure to monitor, arrest and deport immigrants en masse, Hussein and Kim wrote. Gates’s essay in August and interview on Sunday were two of his first major forays into the public since becoming ensnared in the scandal surrounding Jeffrey Epstein, the disgraced financier who pleaded guilty in 2008 to procuring a minor for prostitution before dying by suicide while incarcerated on sex-trafficking charges 11 years later. An external review commissioned by Gates’s philanthropic foundation and released in July determined that he was among a number of organization staffers and leaders who had collectively held about 30 meetings with Epstein from 2011 to 2014. Gates has not been accused of involvement in Epstein’s admitted or alleged crimes. He has said he regretted “every minute” he spent with Epstein, and remains the chair of the $89bn (£65bn) Gates Foundation charity. In a lighter moment during Welker’s interview with Gates, the host asked him: “Are there any ways in which you, professionally or personally, avoid AI and say that: ‘I’m not going to consult with it in this instance?’” Gates, with a chuckle and a smile, replied: “Well, I’m not using it for my personal relationships. I’m not like: ‘Hey, do you like me? Hey, am I a nice guy?’ “So I just never went down that path, because I’m lucky in terms of my family, friends and everything. I don’t socialize with the AI. It knows I’m a very serious person.”

events.title: Couples are using a viral AI agent to do their emotional labor. It’s been helpful — and chaotic.
events.summary: Some early adopters of Instinct are using AI agents to manage common tasks in a relationship, like shared to-do lists and vacation itineraries. It's had mixed results. Getty Images; BI Instinct's new "Trusted Person" allows users to connect their AI agents and tag-team tasks. Some couples use it for shared to-dos or help planning surprise date nights. While it cuts down on emotional labor, a therapist says not so fast: You still have to put work in. AI agents aren't just sneaking into your workplace anymore. Soon, they might be making regular appearances in your relationship. Since the launch of Instinct, an invite-only AI assistant that went viral among Silicon Valley insiders in August, early adopters have been using it to offload tasks like booking hotels and scheduling appointments. Then, on September 9, Noah Shinn, the company's 23-year-old founder, announced Instinct's new "Trusted Person" feature: You could now have your Instinct agent directly communicate with another person's Instinct agent to reduce the amount of "back-and-forth" in a relationship , such as coordinating plans and organizing vacations. Introducing our Trusted Person network powered by our new Instinct-to-Instinct communication protocol. Your Instinct can now talk to other Instincts to coordinate plans on your behalf. Getting people together often involves a lot of back-and-forth: finding a time, working out… pic.twitter.com/LXkDpXGmea — Noah Shinn (@noahrshinn) September 9, 2026 So far, some users have found it helpful. "Instinct syncs with my wife's Instinct so we can actually finish a shared to-do list," Alex Borkin, a 36-year-old entrepreneur who uses AI across his portfolio of companies, said on X , noting that it was easier than manually setting up AI agents using Claude Code or Codex. Have you used Instinct's "Trusted Person" feature with a spouse or partner? If you'd like to share your story, please reach out to jpugachevsky@businessinsider.com. While Instinct may help eradicate the most annoying part of a partnership (figuring out dinner plans when you both keep saying "whatever you want!"), it can also open up the possibilities of new relationship drama. Some users have already reported some issues, ranging from privacy concerns to accidentally spoiled surprises. Your emotional labor robot Emotional labor is disproportionately felt by women in relationships, causing friction. AI agents are marketed as reducing some of those responsibilities. janiecbros/Getty Images The greatest appeal of Instinct and other AI agents is their ability to cut down on what Borkin calls "boring tasks" — like booking appointments or getting refunds. "I close the loop," Borkin told Business Insider. "I get to go to bed and not think of 'Did I take care of jury duty?'" Like other working parents , Borkin and his wife use Instinct's Trusted Person feature to smooth out their day-to-day life as a family with two kids, ages 3 and 20 months (and a third child on the way). Most recently, the couple used Instinct agents to send them individual reminders to complete tasks for their daughter's third birthday party, such as ordering food. "It's nice not having to remind myself of something I asked my wife to help with, and then remind her if she's taking care of it," Borkin said. The more invisible work within a relationship — such as nudging a spouse to finish a task you asked them to do — requires cognitive and emotional labor . Some partners, more often women, can feel as though they bear the brunt of this work, leading to tension in the relationship. Annie Wright, a licensed psychotherapist who works with Silicon Valley clientele , told Business Insider that this dynamic is so common in heterosexual relationships that, sometimes, even AI agents don't fully solve the problem. "Even when you have an AI agent, who's putting in the prompt to begin with, who's architecting out the idea, who's remaining responsible for the oversight of that agent?" Wright said. More often than not, she said it's her female clients who are tasked with the burden. Wright said it can also be tempting to use AI agents as a way to avoid enduring "weaponized incompetence" when a partner performs the task wrong — or just keeps ignoring you. "An AI agent isn't going to bring that same relational scar tissue into the dynamic with you," she said. "It's very compelling. It provides a kind of shortcut, but it doesn't eliminate all the work for you." Deep intimacy required To book flights or fulfill shopping requests, AI agents need access to your credit card and all relevant login credentials. showcake/Getty Images Instinct fans have used it to do everything from booking a birthday cabin to canceling forgotten subscriptions, impressed by its ability to successfully follow through on semi-complex tasks. Users can send Instinct a simple text request to book an in-network doctor's appointment, and it seems to follow through effectively. There's a catch, though: Instinct needs to know a lot about you to perform well. Depending on what you ask it to do, it might need access to your email account, calendar, or even credit card . Users have reported troubling incidents, including privacy and security concerns. Some users have also reported hallucinations and what appeared to be leaks of strangers' data. Out of caution, Borkin said he only linked Instinct to his retailer accounts (like Amazon and Costco) without directly giving it his credit card. He also uses a throwaway email account for Instinct to avoid the risk of any sensitive information being breached. Naturally, AI agent mishaps can cause new issues in a relationship. Wright said the biggest risk is one person in the relationship now feeling responsible for checking that the AI agent properly followed through on instructions. "One partner thinks they've handed off a task while the other partner still feels responsible for making sure it happens — now you've got a new argument," she said. "Technology can become another place where you're disagreeing about who's responsible." When agents remove agency Wright said AI agents can mirror 1950s secretaries, buying anniversary gifts for wives. George Marks/Getty Images Sometimes, Instinct's glitches can be more innocuous — even entertaining. Luba Yudasina, an angel investor, said she asked her Instinct to help her plan a surprise for her boyfriend, according to her post on X . She wanted it to ask him when he was free and what kinds of dates he would like. Instead, it blabbed too much. Told my Instinct to reach out to my bf's Instict to plan a surprise. This is what his Instict texted him 🤪 pic.twitter.com/JqEM2IbzXm — luba yudasina (@LubaYudasina) September 15, 2026 On a bigger scale, using Instinct raises questions about the merits of smoothing out every crease in a relationship. events.title: I left 2 corporate careers to find purpose in Silicon Valley. Instead, I found it solving the wrong things
events.summary: Purpose at work—everyone wants it. But people go to differing lengths to find it. I walked away from a career in law, followed by a stretch in management consultancy, before landing in technology to try and locate more meaning. As a lawyer, I was a fish out of water. The pace, the risk-aversion, the gatekeeping — I felt constantly ill at ease among people who clearly felt right at home. My stint as a consultant ended in me being let go, and left me with the same existential question: could this really be it? So I trusted my instinct and wound my way into startups. In a short period of time, I was running a successful venture-backed parking startup. It gave me the speed, ownership and creativity I’d been looking for, but a question about meaning still lingered. As company CEO, I traveled to San Francisco often: meeting people, raising money, attending events. But on one occasion, I accidentally wandered into the Tenderloin, the city’s notorious downtown neighborhood. It was Christmas Day, bitingly cold, and I chanced upon an open-air church service. On paper, that might sound quaint. In reality, it was the most desolate scene I’ve encountered. People not wearing shoes, human unmentionables littering the pavement. This scene would have been shocking in any city on earth. But I wasn’t in just any city — I was in San Francisco, where one in every 14,000 residents is a billionaire. I tried to square this in my head. When I couldn’t, I realized it was time for another job change — this time, to build a very different kind of business. The problems we chose to solve instead In the decade since that trip to San Francisco, inequality has widened. Meanwhile, the technology industry has done next to nothing to address the most urgent of human problems. What it has done — both brilliantly and expensively — is solve the problems of the people who didn’t have many in the first place. Billions of dollars’ worth of this generation’s finest engineering talent has helped make takeouts arrive quicker while applying the cutting-edge machine learning to serve ads faster and more profitably. I don’t sneer at any of these developments — I ran a parking app, after all, and I’m glad that my food arrives quickly and conveniently, but it raises a question that we don’t ask ourselves enough. Why does so much effort go towards making our already comfortable lives more convenient, all while so little goes towards the people who are most underserved? What we were ignoring While Silicon Valley was making some lives more convenient, many lives got a lot more difficult. In the fiscal year of 2025, SNAP served an average of 42.1 million people every single month. That amounts to 12.3% of the U.S. population — roughly one in eight people in the richest country in history — needing help to buy their food. Now consider how that level of support is administered. In the fiscal year of 2025 the USDA reported a national payment error rate of 10.62 percent , worth $10.1 billion in improper payments. That’s more than one dollar in every ten. When broken down, around 87 percent of that was overpayment, but that leaves roughly 13 per cent as underpayment. That translates as eligible families not getting the support that they are owed. The USDA is explicit that this is not fraud — these are errors, a truth that is constantly misreported in the media. So, what is causing so many errors? Overwhelmingly, they are the result of inordinate amounts of paperwork, outdated systems, handwritten notes, and sheer human exhaustion. Clearly, this is a systems problem. And what’s brilliant at fixing systems problems? Silicon Valley’s favorite friend: software. The bit the spreadsheets miss Behind every one of those error rates are people sitting on either side of a desk. One is seeking support, the other is administering it. A federal study by the Administration for Children and Families published in 2025 found that child welfare caseworkers spend an average of 4.3 hours a day on paperwork and documentation; over half of a standard eight-hour shift. That translates as recruiting people whose entire vocation is centered on sitting with a family in crisis, and then forcing them to spend two thirds of their working life filling out forms. We then act surprised when they grow tired, burn out and leave the profession altogether; national average annual caseworker turnover in U.S. child welfare runs at around 30% (roughly 3 in 10). And the person who needed them often slips through a crack that a better-designed system would have helped prevent. Ten years ago, soon after that defining trip to San Francisco, I gave up on building convenience technology and started building technology for social services instead. Now, I create AI tools for people on the front line and for the vulnerable people that they serve, both of whom the technology sector has widely neglected. For the last decade, my mission has been simple: to put technology — and now AI — at the service of society. Today we’re operating across five countries and in some of the largest cities in the world, including in California. Our first U.S. partner was Fairfax County, Virginia, and today agencies in a dozen U.S. states are cutting the admin burden in half . But this is about so much more than efficiency. This is about supporting thousands of frontline staff in a sector where burnout is commonplace, ensuring that every conversation is documented thoroughly, and ultimately making sure that more vulnerable people get the support they need. Who technology forgot These days most of my time goes on one thing: persuading people who have technical skill to point it at something that matters. It’s the conversation I wish I’d had earlier in my career. There was a time in the early days of the Internet when tech saw itself as being in service of something bigger than itself. Somewhere along the way, that gave way to a race for profit. By measure of money, Silicon Valley has never done better. But it won’t rediscover purpose by solving the inconveniences of people who are already comfortable. The hardest problems facing humanity are unglamorous, badly funded, stifled by bureaucracy and full of forms. But they are also right there, in plain sight, on a freezing pavement just round the corner from the money. events.title: UK police evacuate homes near RAF Fairford airbase used by US
events.summary: Police say they have arrested several men on suspicion of explosives-related offences and bomb disposal experts are examining vehicles. Police have evacuated homes near an airbase in the United Kingdom used by the United States military and arrested several men on suspicion of explosives-related offences. “The army’s specialist explosive ordnance disposal team are currently ⁠examining a number of vehicles,” Gloucestershire police said on Sunday, adding that “a major incident” had been declared. list 1 of 3 Northern Ireland protesters block Orange Order march in Portadown list 2 of 3 What next for Man City as fallout from 115 charges rumbles – all to know list 3 of 3 Pro-Palestine Action group to rally at Labour conference led by Burnham Residents from a number of properties in Whelford, southwestern England, were being taken to a nearby leisure centre. Police said several men had been arrested “on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act”. The town is located near RAF Fairford, an airbase that US forces have used for strikes during the US-Israel war on Iran. A reporter from the Reuters news agency at the scene said armed police had blocked access to the base’s main gate, while equipment had been placed in front of entry points. About 30 emergency vehicles, including police cars, ambulances and fire engines, were stationed in the nearby town of Fairford. Gloucestershire police said in a statement they would like “to reassure people that we believe this incident is contained”. Britain’s Defence Secretary Wes Streeting thanked the emergency and specialist teams who responded to the incident. “We can be reassured that this is being dealt with,” he said. Prime Minister Andy Burnham is receiving updates on the situation, his office said. Local media said counter-terrorism police were leading the investigation. There was no immediate information about what prompted the arrests, whether explosives were found, or if the suspected offences were connected to the airbase. The US Air Force said it was aware of reports about the incident but declined to discuss specific security measures. A spokesperson said the 501st Combat Support Wing, a US Air Force unit in Britain, and other US units based in the UK remained vigilant and would take steps needed to protect personnel and their families. In March, three US B-1B Lancer bombers touched down at RAF Fairford after what is believed to be the first US strike mission against Iran launched from a British base, during the war on Iran. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, a powerful military force that operates alongside the country’s regular armed forces, warned in July that bases used to launch attacks on Iran could be treated as legitimate targets. Authorities have not linked Sunday’s arrests to Iran or said RAF Fairford was a target.

events.title: Iran shifts trade north to Caspian Sea as war impairs Strait of Hormuz
events.summary: Iran is looking for alternatives to export its oil as the US blockades its southern ports. Tehran, Iran – With Iran’s southern ports subject to a United States naval blockade, Tehran is looking for alternatives to export oil and import goods. The Caspian Sea on Iran’s northern coast is seen as one portal for Iran to the outside world. Recent efforts at the United Nations to end the deadlock between Iran and the US appear to have failed as US President Donald Trump said Tehran’s offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz was unacceptable. With no breakthrough in sight on ending the war launched by the US and Israel on Iran on February 28, Tehran is making adjustments to export oil and import essential goods. But maritime trade via the Caspian Sea has its own logistical challenges, experts said. The Caspian Sea, the world’s largest landlocked body of water, is shared by Iran, Russia, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan. Shipping on the sea has been increasingly challenged by declining water levels in recent years. In April, UN Environment Programme Executive Director Inger Andersen said Caspian water levels had dropped by about 2 metres (6.6ft) since the 1990s. Sea levels are projected to recede by an additional 8 to 21 metres (26ft to 69ft) by the end of the century. Shahram Fadakar, director general of the Iranian Department of Environment’s Office for Coastal and Marine Ecosystem Protection, told local media last week that water levels have been dropping by more than 20cm (7.9 inches) annually over the past two to three years. This could affect trade between all Caspian countries, including Iran. This month, Masoud Polmeh, secretary-general of the Shipping Association of Iran, told state-linked media that Iran’s northern ports could once handle berth vessels weighing up to 6,000 tonnes. Due to reduced water levels, they can now handle only 4,000-tonne vessels. Iranian ships entering the Caspian Sea via Russia’s Volga River have become stuck due to low water levels, sometimes remaining stationary for days and weeks at a time before their crews are rescued. “Fortunately, that hasn’t happened in our ports,” Polmeh added. The vast majority of Iran’s maritime trade has been conducted via its southern ports, but the US naval embargo and air strikes on infrastructure are forcing Tehran to shift trade to the Caspian Sea and its land borders. While there are currently no active military attacks against interests in the north, Vali Kaleji, an independent writer and researcher in Iran on Russia, Central Asia and the Caucasus, said changes in logistical operations have put huge strains on Iran’s land borders. At the Norduz border crossing with Armenia, as many as 1,800 trucks queue for several days at a time to enter Iran. At other terminals, wait times range from 10 to 15 days to enter Iran although Kaleji said this is not due solely to freight shifting to Iran’s roads. “Limited terminal capacity, customs procedures, road infrastructure and ongoing construction projects have also contributed to the congestion. Meanwhile, sanctions on Iranian airlines and the resulting influx of passengers towards Iran’s land borders with Armenia and Turkey have further exacerbated problems at the border terminals,” Kaleji told Al Jazeera. The eastern Caspian rail route provides a connection for transporting Iranian cargo to Turkmenistan, Kazakhstan and China. But Iran’s rail freight connections with the South Caucasus region, which were severed during the First Nagorno-Karabakh War from 1988 to 1994, remain closed. “The revival of the Julfa-Nakhchivan railway route, part of the Soviet-era railway network in the South Caucasus, also depends on the peace process between Armenia and Azerbaijan, particularly the implementation of the TRIPP project,” Kaleji said, referring to a US-supported transit corridor in the region. “Since a major share of transit and trade along the western route of the North-South Transport Corridor takes place through this route, the absence of a railway connection between Iran and the South Caucasus remains a major obstacle to accelerating and increasing the volume of trade and transit, particularly under conditions of intensified maritime blockade in the south.” Iranian authorities have not provided details on which commodities and at what volume trade has been directed northwards, including to the Caspian ports of Anzali, Amirabad and Nowshahr. But there have been indications of such a shift, particularly with the import of essential goods, such as food. Last month, Ports and Maritime Organization chief Mohammad Shakibi-Nasab told state-linked media that Iran’s total nominal port capacity was 300 million tonnes, only 30 million tonnes of which is linked to its northern ports. The northern ports’ share of essential goods transport has gone up from 18 percent in the years before the US-Israel war on Iran to 30 percent today.

events.title: Photos: Pope Leo draws hundreds of thousands for open-air Mass in Paris
events.summary: Pope Leo XIV celebrates an open-air mass for hundreds of thousands of believers on the Champs Elysees. Hundreds of thousands of people packed Paris’s iconic Champs-Elysees to attend an open-air Mass led by Pope Leo XIV. The Vatican said about 800,000 people were at the service on Saturday – roughly 200,000 more than those who had registered in advance. The pope greeted flag-waving, cheering crowds from his popemobile during a 2km (1.2-mile) parade along the grand boulevard leading to Place de la Concorde. An imposing stage built for the mass, topped with a golden cross, and row upon row of choir singers, clergy and worshippers praying under the pope’s gaze on Place de la Concorde marked a new chapter for the history-steeped square that was an execution site during the French Revolution. Louis XVI and Marie-Antoinette were guillotined there. For many in France, it embodies the republic and traditionally stages Bastille Day celebrations. Organisers say it is the only site in central Paris able to hold such large crowds. But the choice of location has drawn criticism from supporters of France’s strict secularism in public life, rooted in a 1905 law separating church and state. They argue that Place de la Concorde symbolises the republic, and that other venues, such as Les Invalides, the complex where Pope Benedict XVI celebrated mass with 240,000 people in 2008, would have been more appropriate.

events.title: Gen Z aren’t ready for the workplace—and this youth job program CEO is giving them a crash course in emails and workplace etiquette to change that
events.summary: Gen Zers are eager to land their first internships and full-time jobs, but getting a foot in the door has become increasingly difficult for many. Employers say the youngest class of corporate workers aren’t equipped to thrive in today’s workplace—so one youth employment program is trying to bridge the gap before they even graduate high school. National nonprofit Genesys Works has been helping underserved high schoolers land their first work opportunities since 2002. The organization prepares students for professional careers with skills training, long-term coaching, and paid corporate internships to get their feet wet. But before they step into roles at one of Genesys’ hundreds of partner companies including Accenture , JPMorgan, and Mayo Clinic, the next generation of workers undergoes an eight-week summer program, learning skills like communication, critical thinking, digital literacy, Excel, and office etiquette. The crash course not only sets up Genesys Works participants with greater confidence to enter the workforce, their training also sets them apart from the rest. While managers complain of Gen Z workers lacking interpersonal, professional, and technical skills, these budding professionals are prepared to step into a work life they may have never been exposed to. “I don’t believe [it] when employers say that they can’t find the talent. The challenge is they do want someone who’s ready to go to work,” Byron V. Garrett, the CEO of Genesys Works, tells Fortune , adding that “Oftentimes our young professionals don’t come from backgrounds where folks call [their] mom or aunt and say, ‘Hey, I ran into this problem at work. What do I do?’…Because they don’t know anyone who actually has done that before.” The eight-week crash course teaches Gen Zers the workplace basics and AI The summer before their senior year of high school, teenagers across Genesys’ nine regional markets undergo universal training. They learn how to prepare resumes and develop their LinkedIn pages, sitting through mock interviews to fine-tune their speaking skills. The Gen Zers are taught to keep their phones away during meetings, ditch abbreviations in their emails, and keep on top of meeting documents. The CEO says that “core professional skills” including critical thinking, logic, and reasoning, have “become so important right now.” “[Employers] may not be looking for practical skill sets related to the actual position,” Garrett explains. “We’re giving you those office professional skills so that you know what it means to go to work, to be on time, to report into a structure.” On top of mastering etiquette and learning the basics that will serve them well in the office, the higher schoolers also dig deeper into AI. Oftentimes, schools haven’t added the tech into their curriculum, so Garrett says the program is stepping in. The digital natives are already deeply familiar with chatbots, but Genesys teaches the importance of fact-checking the work, knowing limitations around AI, and protecting proprietary information.  “We also give you the other technical skills,” he continued. “Let’s make you proficient in the office suite…How do we now help you understand how to use AI? Not just from a personal perspective, but how do you improve business efficiency utilizing prompt engineering? You can [use] Chat[GPT], but here’s a way to do that in the context of business.” Over the past two decades, Genesys has served more than 14,000 students nationwide, and in 2025 alone, it helped 2,161 teenagers launch their professional careers. The non-profit has worked with 205 corporate partners across 27 industries, including healthcare, technology, finance, and construction. And the program is leading to monetary wins that extend beyond the first paycheck. While unpaid internships have become the status quo for young workers, Genesys only places students into paid gigs, and can earn up to $14,000 during their senior-year internship. Garrett says it gives them a “different sense of dignity,” especially as money is tight for many Americans. Alumni who are seven or more years out of the program earn an average salary of $67,000 per year. Meanwhile, the typical starting salary for similarly-aged recent college graduates rests at just $56,153, according to 2026 data from Clever. Genesys estimates that 73% of surveyed alumni earn more than at least one of their parents—and 20% even own a home. Healthcare and construction companies are all-in on Gen Z talent Gen Zers have struggled to land entry-level work as employers have reeled back hiring, creating a pressure-cooker of competition. Garrett says that some companies partnering with Genesys have had to tighten their belts, but there are still bright spots for young talent.  The CEO says that employers in healthcare have ramped up hiring of Genesys-trained teenagers. Mayo Clinic’s campus in Jacksonville, Florida has doubled the number of interns in their cohort this new cycle, and Garrett has witnessed a surge in demand as physical construction ramps up. While the interns aren’t doing hard-hat work on site, they’re taking on back office, procurement, and quality assurance gigs. Genesys is also looking at growing industries they want to be competitive in; as AI data centers spring up across the country, Garrett says there’s an opportunity to help fill the shortage of data engineers and HVAC technicians. But the biggest opportunity has continued to be the tech sector, the CEO says. With companies increasingly looking for workers who can navigate both technology and the office environment, Garrett says Genesys-trained students bring both technical skills and professional experience to the table. “Where we’ve had the most success historically [is with] folks who really want a career in technology,” Garrett says. “They really see us as a viable opportunity for that, because there have been so many young professionals that have gone on to work at the IT help desk.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Baby bank's urgent appeal as demand for help grows
events.summary: Chantal Nogbou founded Leeds Baby Bank in 2017 and the charity marks its first decade in January The founder of a charity which provides essentials like Moses baskets, prams, nappies and clothes to struggling families across Leeds has said it urgently needs more donations to help keep up with demand. Chantal Nogbou said there had been a "massive increase" in the number of people referred by health and social care professionals to Leeds Baby Bank in recent months. Nogbou said staff had helped an "unprecedented" 550 families in Leeds since the start of June, and were expecting numbers to rise as winter loomed. "We get even more people needing help then because they want to put the heating on, but they still need to buy nappies and feed and clothe their child," she said. Nogbou founded Leeds Baby Bank in 2017 when she was a single parent of four children, including twins, and she realised how many other families were struggling. More families than ever have been referred to Leeds Baby Bank for help since the start of June, according to the charity The charity will be 10 years old in January and Nogbou said that staff had seen a change in the families who needed their support over time. "When we started, pre-Covid, maybe one in five children in Leeds lived in relative poverty," she explained. "Now, you're looking at one in two children in some parts, and that's just a shocking number that really shouldn't be happening." Nogbou said that about 70% of the children they helped had a parent who was working and she said many were "not managing to manage the bills with energy and fuel prices going up". According to government statistics, 27% of children in the Yorkshire and Humber region lived in relative low income families - the joint highest proportion, alongside the West Midlands, in the country. A relative low income family is one living on less than 60% of the median national household income for that year. Chantal Nogbou said people did not realise how far a small financial donation could go Nogbou said the rise in referrals meant more financial challenges for the charity, especially after moving from a city centre office to a larger and more accessible building in Armley which could now provide more services. "All that has cost money and obviously bills for us have also gone up when it comes to the utilities, so it's definitely a scary thing as a charity," she said. She added that it was the donations of items and money from the community that had kept the charity going. "It's the people that, instead of buying a coffee every day, set up a direct debit and send £5 to Leeds Baby Bank every month," she said. events.title: How Trump could wrest Citgo from Elliott Management and hand it back to Venezuela
events.summary: Early this year, it seemed all but certain that Citgo Petroleum—the Houston oil refiner familiar to American drivers, but little known as a Venezuelan subsidiary—was about to fall into the hands of a U.S. activist hedge fund . In November 2025, a Delaware federal judge  ordered the sale of the company to Elliott Management and its affiliate startup, Amber Energy. The court ruled that Citgo could be held liable for the Venezuelan government’s debts, and approved a sale that would send $9 billion to pay off a small number of Venezuela’s numerous creditors. All that was needed to close the sale was a green light from the Trump administration, at which point Citgo and its U.S. refineries would come under American ownership for the first time in nearly 40 years.   In the weeks after the dramatic ouster of former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro in early January, that approval appeared close at hand. Energy Secretary Chris Wright applauded the forced sale to Elliott and its GOP megadonor founder, Paul Singer. It was seen as a win-win deal. The court-ordered sale—opposed by the Venezuelan government—would reduce Venezuela’s massive debt pile while giving a U.S. company the opportunity to expand the Gulf Coast’s refining capacity, including churning more Venezuelan crude, which could help drive down gas prices. “I think that’s fantastic,” Wright said.   But eight months later, that approval is nowhere in sight. The Treasury Department has extended Citgo’s protection from the sale six times since January, raising questions over whether November’s court-ordered sale to one of Trump’s wealthiest allies could be undone by geopolitics. After all, a now U.S.-friendly interim Venezuelan government still doesn’t want to give up its crown-jewel assets in Citgo, and the Trump administration may be more amenable to that sentiment from Caracas. “There’s an open question now as to whether or not the Citgo sale is a requirement,” said Richard Nephew, a sanctions expert at Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy who helped broker sanctions negotiations in the Obama administration.   Keeping in place Citgo’s protection from being sold avoids disrupting the ongoing cooperation between the U.S. and Venezuela, said Jose Ignacio Hernandez, a Harvard law professor and former special counsel for Venezuelan opposition leader Juan Guaidó. The Trump administration’s public policy towards Venezuela is the three-step strategy espoused by Secretary of State Marco Rubio—stabilization, recovery and transition. “Any license authorizing the [Citgo] sale order will definitely disrupt these three phases,” Hernandez said. Hedge fund versus state oil The ongoing delay allows Venezuela to strengthen its last-ditch effort to save its cash cow from Elliott’s clutches. Attorneys representing Venezuela and its state-owned oil company, PDVSA, appealed Delaware District Judge Leonard Stark’s sale order, arguing the court-appointed neutral adviser, who designed the auction process and selected Elliott’s winning bid, wasn’t so neutral. The appeals court should vacate the sale order, PDVSA and a rival bidder argue, because the adviser hired outside consulting firms that had earned $170 million in fees from clients tied to Elliott. Oral arguments are scheduled for October.   But the 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals hasn’t ruled favorably to the Venezuelan parties in nearly a decade of attempts. The higher court has a streak of affirming Stark’s rulings or dismissing Venezuela’s challenges to his decisions, causing skepticism among several legal analysts about Venezuela’s prospects for victory. A denial would place the fate of Citgo, its three U.S. refineries, and its pipeline network solely in the hands of the Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), which can grant a sale license and deprive Venezuela of its most valuable asset, or deny the license and allow Citgo to be a part of the nation’s revitalization. So long as the decision hangs in the balance, the Trump administration can wield Citgo as a key piece of leverage in its dealings with Venezuela’s interim president, Delcy Rodriguez. “What does Trump gain if he keeps the [Citgo] protection in place? He gets a bargaining chip that is very powerful, that says, ‘Don’t deviate from this path or you’ll pay for it,’” said Jose Enrique Arrioja, senior director of policy at the Council of the Americas. “It gives you big leverage in negotiating with that partner.”  Treating Citgo as a bargaining chip may prove useful when dealing with an interim government still led by the Chavista political machinery, which has ruled Venezuela and defied U.S. hegemony in the region since the turn of the century.  Rodriguez, whose hold on power depends on support from the Trump administration, has all but become a Trump proxy for now as she navigates this delicate diplomatic moment. Yet the Chavismo political apparatus she commands remains nearly intact. In March, Rodriguez appointed Asdrúbal Chávez, cousin of the former president, Hugo Chávez, to lead Citgo’s parent company despite his U.S. visa being revoked in 2018. Recently, OFAC issued a rule preventing any further leadership changes to Citgo and its parent companies.  “Now, the interest is trying to make sure Venezuelan oil is getting to market, and we get our cut, and that Delcy is in a position to do whatever we want,” Columbia University’s Nephew said. Citgo’s dual status Reminders of Citgo’s dual citizenship abound outside the company’s corporate headquarters in Houston, where a Venezuelan flag flies alongside the stars and stripes. Citgo, a company founded 116 years ago in Oklahoma, saw 50% of its stake purchased by PDVSA in 1986 and the remainder in 1990 to secure its access to the U.S. market. The Venezuelan national oil company quickly upgraded Citgo’s two Gulf Coast refineries to process Venezuela’s distinct grade of heavy sour oil.  By the early 2000s, Citgo was refining roughly one-third of all Venezuelan oil exports to the U.S., transforming the nation’s raw, peanut butter-like crude into fuels, petrochemicals and asphalt. Citgo’s refineries in Texas, Louisiana, and Illinois were producing&nb

events.title: ‘People are standing up and fighting back’: the north Devon revolt against a vast AI datacentre
events.summary: Plans for one of Europe’s largest AI campuses in a Unesco-designated reserve have sparked a fierce local backlash The datacentre revolt spreading across the US has reached the rolling hills of north Devon in an uprising against a planned hyperscale AI data campus in the middle of a globally protected landscape. Perched on an inland cliff, the town of Great Torrington has views that stretch for miles over the landscape of the Unesco biosphere reserve in which it sits, taking in the winding River Torridge and rolling acres of wooded valley and wildflower meadows. Pastoral and peaceful, its history was notably punctured by violence in 1646 when the royalists’ resistance in the first English civil war was brought to an end by the parliamentarian New Model Army in a battle fought out in the narrow streets in heavy rain and darkness. Today, a very 21st-century threat is rippling through the same country lanes as the AI boom reaches the pubs, churches and parish halls of Great Torrington and its surrounding villages. The countryside that makes up the biosphere has been selected by a British company, Xlinks, to house a 1.5GW AI datacentre, one of the largest in Europe, as well as a vast 1.8GW battery energy storage system, or BESS. About 344 hectares (850 acres) of countryside have been secured for the huge campus, with five vast buildings ranging in height from 50 to 130 feet. Listed buildings on the site, Xlinks says, will be relocated and transformed into a visitor centre. Such is the anger locally that the new campaign against the AI datacentre has drawn in tens of thousands of people, uncovered what campaigners say is evidence of secret deals and adopted tactics being used by activists in the US such as Erin Brockovich . A recent public meeting in Great Torrington was hosted by Elizabeth Humphreys of the US campaign group Not in My Valley . She was one of the forces behind achieving a permanent datacentre ban in Coachella, California, over concerns about air pollution, water and energy use. “We’re fighting the largest companies that have ever existed in the world, and that is scary but we are all fighting this together,” Humphreys said. “This is a global issue; we are all connected. People across the world are standing up and fighting back.” Today within the halls and pubs of Great Torrington and the villages of Huntshaw and Weare Giffard, the AI project is the main talking point. And the question being asked is: why here, in a protected UN biosphere, on productive farmland? The proposal was first announced to the public this summer with a call by Xlinks for a collaborative approach. But adopting the tactics of veteran campaigners like Brockovich, people from the Devon Datacentre and BESS action group took to their keyboards – researching, rallying and requesting more information in a series of freedom of information (FoI) applications. What they uncovered fuelled the rising tensions. Documents released under FoI revealed the company had been in closed discussions with council officials since March 2025. In April, the council issued a letter of “in-principle support” before any environmental statement or public consultation – and more than a year before the proposal was made public. Torridge district council told the Guardian the pre-application process was standard practice and was confidential. A spokesperson said it was not confirmation of any proposal and intended to offer guidance on whether a proposal was acceptable in principle in planning terms. In an email dated 18 December 2025, council officials and the developers discussed creating links with a sixth form college in Exeter and a stakeholder engagement plan. “Who do we all feel it is critical to get onboard and when both locally and further afield?” the email asked. Emily Clark, of the Devon Datacentre and BESS action group, said: “Email exchanges and private meetings spanning the past 18 months reveal some officers treating the project as a foregone conclusion. Community frustration is understandably at boiling point. “How can the largest and most costly infrastructure proposal in the nation be conducted almost exclusively in secret?” FoI requests also uncovered a detailed site plan not released to the public. It revealed the two largest buildings would measure 335 metres by 267 metres and cover approximately nine hectares (22 acres) of ground footprint each – both big enough to house Exeter Cathedral 18 times over, campaigners say. Xlinks said its proposals cover about 344 hectares (850 acres) but only a third would be developed; the majority of land would be open to the public or used for new habitat creation to support wildlife, they said. The campus would also house a 1.8GW battery energy storage system (BESS) involving 1,720 containerised units, dwarfing the largest operational BESS currently in Britain, such as the 100MW Bramley facility in Hampshire.

events.title: Trump rejects Iran’s seven-day peace deal to reopen strait of Hormuz
events.summary: US president is said to expect renewed strikes after the midterms Donald Trump has said he has rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the strait of Hormuz within a week and resume nuclear talks in return for the lifting of the US naval blockade of Iranian ports. “They made a proposal but I reject it,” the US president told reporters at the White House. The president was earlier said to be privately sceptical Iran would meet his demands to dismantle its nuclear programme, according to unnamed US officials cited by the Wall Street Journal. Trump has told aides he expects to resume bombing Iran after the November midterms in the US, the newspaper reported. Meanwhile, on Friday evening, he published a post on his Truth Social platform with a graphic showing a map with the strait of Hormuz renamed as the “Trump Strait”. During a three-hour meeting at the UN general assembly in New York earlier this week, Iran had proposed reopening the strait, which would relieve pressure on global energy markets, and restart talks on its nuclear programme within seven days. In return, as well as lifting its naval blockade, Iran wants the US to permit the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets, restore the waiver that lifted sanctions on Iran’s oil exports and observe a “ceasefire on all fronts”. That would involve the US president convincing Israel to end its attacks on Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon, a tall order, and allowing the strait to reopen largely on Iran’s terms, with the new route predominantly going through Iranian waters. Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, on Sunday said “our conditions are clear and any move toward reopening the strait of Hormuz is contingent upon these conditions being fulfilled”. “We will not back down from them,” Araghchi said, state broadcaster IRIB reported. “We have never closed the door to diplomacy or negotiations, but at the same time, we have never backed down from our rights.” Reports of the rejection came as Iranian state media reported on Saturday morning that the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, was on his way back to Tehran from New York. After a meeting with UN secretary general, António Guterres, Pezeshkian said: “Iran has not walked away from the negotiating table, but given past experiences, it no longer trusts the United States.” Araghchi said on Sunday that the Iranians “saw the first reaction from the US president, but so far, nothing has been conveyed to us by the mediators”. “We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive positions to us, and we will make a decision based on them,” the foreign minister added. Earlier, a US official had ⁠said discussions with Iran through mediators were “positive and constructive” and, on Friday, Araghchi, had detailed the proposal to reporters outside the UN security council. He said the seven-day timeline to open the strait and resume talks could start as soon as the US accepts Iran’s proposal. The initial steps would take about four to five days to complete, the strait would be opened on the sixth day and talks on the nuclear programme would start on the seventh day, he said. This would include a protocol to allow UN nuclear inspectors back in to look at Iran’s damaged sites and the stockpile of highly enriched uranium. The US naval blockade is putting intense pressure on the Iranian economy, while the seven-month-old conflict in the region has disrupted oil flows through one of the world’s most critical shipping lanes and is increasing the cost of living around the globe. Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show Face the Nation, said Tehran was ready for talks on its nuclear programme and other issues, but would not accept “bullying or coercion”. “Iran is not seeking war, but will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that “we’re not supposed to develop nuclear weapons”. Previous attempts at diplomacy have failed ‌to end the war, which began on 28 February with US and Israeli attacks. Since then the conflict has alternated between pauses and renewed strikes, killing thousands while degrading Iran’s conventional forces and damaging its already ailing economy. Iran and its allies have retaliated by extending the conflict throughout the region. Iran has struck US allies in the Gulf with drones and missiles while its Houthi allies in Yemen have targeted Saudi interests. Iranian-aligned militias in Iraq were blamed for a pipeline attack that temporarily took more Saudi oil off the market. The violence in Yemen has prompted a new humanitarian crisis, the UN children’s agency said on Friday, reporting a rise in acute malnutrition among children. Trump has previously said he was in no rush to reach a deal, even as high oil prices fuel inflation. On the Iranian side, there are questions as to whether the hardliners who dominate the security forces would accept compromises championed by moderates such as Pezeshkian.

events.title: The ecstasy of buying our first home was short-lived after we found 150 faults
events.summary: Charles and Georgina Barnes bought a new build home in February 2026 It was the day Georgina and Charles Barnes had waited three years for, as they picked up the keys to their first home. But when the brand new property was inspected days later by a Welsh snagging company, the final quality check by independent inspectors, they found 150 defects. These included incorrectly installed fire barriers, signs of a previous leak and what they called "exceptionally poor" workmanship. Swansea-based New Home Quality Control was set up by John Cooper, who became fed up of being asked to hide things from customers on building sites. It is the responsibility of developers to make sure new-builds meet regulations, according to the National House Building Council , external (NHBC). The couple are far from alone when it comes to issues with new houses. Written evidence submitted by the New Homes Ombudsman Service said the Home Builders Federation national new homes customer satisfaction survey, published in March 2025, showed 93.7% of new-build buyers reporting defects or snags to their developer after moving in , external . Just over a quarter of buyers also found more than 15 problems in their new-build home. Charles and Georgina were excited to move into their new home "We just wouldn't have known," said Georgina. "If there had been a fire, that's one thing that could have happened and been very detrimental." Georgina, 36, and her husband saved for three years to buy a house, before falling in love with the development in south Leicestershire. As moving day approached, social media began serving her a steady stream of new-build horror stories After paying £299,995 for the house, she said getting it snagged was "non-negotiable". "It just felt unbelievable that we'd finally done it," she added. "We actually finally got our own place. This is ours. This is ours to do what we want with. It just felt great." But the report also identified improperly roofing defects, low water pressure and what inspectors described as "exceptionally poor" installation of the gas meter cabinet and gas pipe. More than a dozen of additional cosmetic and finishing defects were also recorded throughout the property As they had a two-year warranty from the developer, it meant they fixed the issues. John Cooper describes how he came to set up a snagging company "I would say for any new-build buyer, 100% no doubt, I recommend a snagger," Georgina said. Vistry, responsible for the housing developer Countryside, which built Charles and Georgina's house, said it supported "appropriately conducted independent inspections as an additional source of reassurance about build quality". It said each home is checked by its teams and independent inspections take place and, two to three weeks after customers move in, the build team meets to discuss and agree any snagging work. Such issues are not new to John Cooper, 50, co-founder of New Home Quality Control. He said, while working as a contracts manager in 2018: "The site manager asked me to hide something from a customer that was moving in the next day." This was the tip of the iceberg after he had seen poor quality workmanship over about six years. "From that moment on, I thought to myself 'I've got to make a change in this industry somehow. This can't continue'," he said. Cooper spoke to his supervisor at the time, Lee Challenger, 42, and the two men quit their jobs and started New Homes Quality Control. "We've never inspected a house and found absolutely nothing wrong with it," he said. John Cooper was asked to hide issues in new build homes so he created a company to fight back The most common defects involve brickwork, carpentry and roofing, he said. "I just think that there's not enough quality bricklayers to build the amount of properties that the developers are building across the UK on a yearly basis." The team also regularly identifies missing or incorrectly installed weep vents - which are installed in exterior walls to let moisture escape. Cooper said some developments had even featured "fake" weep vents, where decorative plastic pieces had been fitted instead of functioning openings. "They thought they could get away with it," he said. Cooper said before new owners get the keys, the NHBC inspects the property and sign it off. "I'm sick of hearing every property being signed off, because if that was the case, then we wouldn't have a company," he said. Many of Cooper's clients get emotional when they see how many issues there are with their new houses. "There were some quite serious issues in their new property and they had spent all their life savings on it." Cooper said his long-term goal was for every new-build home to undergo an independent inspection before its owners moved in. "If someone's spending their life savings on a house, they deserve to get what they paid for," he said.

events.title: London’s investment bankers and lawyers make more than £1bn in takeover frenzy
events.summary: Bumper fees paid in the year’s mergers and acquisitions spark anger over high City pay during cost of living crisis London’s investment bankers and lawyers have made more than £1bn from a frenzy of takeover deals this year, sparking anger over high City pay during the cost of living crisis . The value of mergers and acquisitions of UK stock market listed companies has surged 175% in 2026 to $132.9bn (£100bn), according to the London Stock Exchange , as overseas buyers snap up British companies at record pace. Fees paid to investment bankers, lawyers and accountants working on these deals topped £1.2bn, official filings suggest, helping drive multimillion-pound pay packets. The bumper fees were fuelled by a string of corporate takeovers driven by a flood of private equity cash and acquisitive American buyers targeting undervalued British businesses. The spree of acquisitions of listed companies has led to concerns over the future of the London stock market . The takeover frenzy has fed advisory business at the biggest banks and law firms in the City. Bankers at JP Morgan have been the busiest, advising on more takeovers involving UK companies than any other bank this year – a total of 14 deals worth a combined $89.4bn (£67.6bn), according to the LSE. The leading law firm was Slaughter and May, it found. UK bankers have also benefited from soaring bonuses, after the government scrapped a rule capping bonuses at two-times annual salaries in late 2023. Each bank now sets its own upward limit. Big investment banks such as Goldman Sachs now allow performers to be paid up to 25 times their annual salary . The surge in business comes while the banking sector lobbies against paying higher taxes in the UK . Jamie Dimon, the billionaire boss of JP Morgan, has issued several warnings to Andy Burnham and his chancellor, John Healey, against raising taxes on banks in his inaugural budget on 28 October. The industry body UK Finance echoed the view this week. Lenders in the UK currently pay a 28% corporation tax rate, higher than the standard 25%, as well as a separate surcharge on their UK balance sheets. The most lucrative deal in the City this year was the £10.6bn takeover of the lab testing group Intertek by the private equity firm EQT, which is expected to generate more than £370m in fees. Morgan Stanley, Barclays and Deutsche Bank are working on the deal for EQT, while Intertek paid Goldman Sachs, JP Morgan Cazenove and PJT Partners. Lawyers at top City firms have started to out-earn some bankers. Partners at the “magic circle” firms Linklaters and Clifford Chance were paid an average of £2.5m and £2.3m respectively in the year to April, their highest ever. A&O Shearman partners were paid £2.2m. At the boutique bank Evercore, which the LSE said had advised on five deals in the UK stock market this year, the firm’s “members” – senior managing directors who are dealmakers – were paid an average of about £2m. Its best-paid member collected £16.2m this year. Overall, dealmaker fees are likely to be even higher this year as the figures do not include deals which did not complete, were rejected or for which documents have not been published – including the £5.7bn takeover of the FTSE 100 airline easyJet by the private equity firm Apollo Global Management, agreed last month . While pay continues to climb in the City, millions of UK households are struggling with the cost of living. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Charlotte Brumpton-Childs, the national secretary at the GMB union, said financial brokers were paid huge sums “while the people who keep this country moving struggle to make ends meet”. “The UK needs to seriously re-examine what we value and hold dear – is it the people who build, who create, who look after us and our loved ones in their hour of need? Or is it a bloated financial sector?” she asked. Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, repeated his call for a windfall tax on lenders’ profits as interest rates have risen , saying that “if banks can afford bonanza payouts for their top brass, they can clearly afford to pay more tax”. “People up and down the country are struggling, and things could get a lot worse with energy prices set to shoot up,” he said. Earlier this month figures from the Office for National Statistics showed that average growth in total earnings, including bonuses, slowed to 3.9% in the three months ended in July, down from 4.1% in the three months ended in June. There are fears that, while dealmakers’ pay is rising on the takeover boom, investment banks could lose out on revenue from their sell-side research and work on flotations as more companies leave London’s stock market and fewer line up to join.

events.title: ‘Mum, where did my Robux go?’ The Roblox scam targeting children
events.summary: Criminals are trying to glean login details to harvest players’ in-game currency and personal data Your 10-year-old son has started playing Roblox , when he realises all of his in-game currency, Robux, is gone. When you try to find out what happened, he says he was recently promised extra Robux if he followed a link on YouTube. When he signed on at the site link, he was taken to the Roblox site as usual but there was no sign of the extra currency. He has fallen victim to a fraud where Roblox users – many of whom are children – are being targeted for their login details. With those details criminals can steal the virtual currency and players’ personal data. Within Roblox, players use Robux to buy virtual items, such as skins or animations for their avatar. You can earn the currency within the game, but it can also be bought. At Roblox’s online store you can buy packages costing up to £199.99 . Using ready-made kits bought on the dark web, fraudsters create a fake login page that is identical in appearance to the legitimate Roblox site. “The kid will enter their details and the fake website will actually redirect them to a legitimate Roblox page,” says Gerald Kasulis, the vice-president of global affairs at the cybersecurity company NordVPN. “So ultimately, the kid will get to where they want to go.” By that stage, however, the criminals will have the details they need for defrauding. Researchers from NordVPN say that over a seven-day period they found almost 200 addresses selling ready-made phishing pages that provided the tools to defraud Roblox users. Often the links to the phishing sites are in comments on YouTube or TikTok videos or in chats on Discord, the chat app for gamers. The message might say there are free Robux available if a player clicks on the link provided. Like many scams, there will often be an element of urgency attached, such as the offer apparently only being valid for a few hours, to encourage the victim to act without fully thinking through the consequences. From that link, the child will be taken to a fake sign-in page that will probably be identical to a legitimate Roblox site in appearance. The address will usually contain the name Roblox, for example “Roblox-verify” or “login-Roblox”. When they are on the scam site, the child will be asked for their username and password but may also be told to put in two-factor identification codes, says NordVPN. But then the child is taken to the legitimate Roblox site so they can play their games as normal, leaving little indication that anything is amiss. Once they have the login details, the fraudster may sell them on or use them to transfer Robux to another account. “One of the simplest habits is to encourage children to open Roblox directly through the official app or website rather than logging in through links they are sent,” says Marijus Briedis, chief technology officer at NordVPN. “Two-factor authentication remains an important protection, but authentication codes and backup codes should be treated just like passwords and never handed over to somebody else.” If your player has lost their Robux to a hacker, it seems unlikely that they will get it back. Roblox says that it is under “no obligation” to assist people whose accounts have been compromised, unless it is required to do so by law. “Roblox does not guarantee that an individual’s account will be restored to its previous state, or that Roblox will be able to recover lost virtual items or virtual currency,” it says. In “very limited circumstances”, Roblox says it may recover lost items or the value of them. A spokesperson for Roblox says there are security measures in place to prevent phishing, such as two-factor authentication and a feature that stops criminals logging into your account from elsewhere. “We continue to work on new ways to minimise the risk of account theft and actively encourage Roblox users to follow security best practices, including not clicking on links or downloading anything from unknown senders or websites,” the spokesperson adds.

events.title: Double the height, 160 times the voltage. The latest ugly side effect of the AI revolution
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Suburban residents protest 15-metre power poles linked to data centre expansion Topic: Urban Development and Planning Industrial power poles 15 metres high have been installed outside Cameron Botterill's house. ( ABC News ) When Cameron Botterill left home one morning, he didn't expect to return to 15-metre power poles soaring above his residential street in Melbourne's inner west. "They're absolute monstrosities," Mr Botterill said. "They're ginormous. They tower above anything else in the suburb and they look very industrial. We're in a residential area here and we definitely did not ask for them to be installed." The power poles went up within a day. ( ABC News ) The new poles are more than twice the height of the 7-metre wooden poles they replaced, and can carry up to 66,000 volts of electricity, roughly 160 times the voltage that previously ran through his street. In July, Mr Botterill was notified by his electricity distributor, Jemena, that the power would be shut off to allow workers to replace the poles on his street. He didn't find out why until the day the new poles appeared. "I was shocked that this could be installed in a residential area." The site of the NextDC data centre in West Footscray. ( ABC News: Kyle Harley ) The NextDC data centre in nearby West Footscray is already operating, and it's being expanded. One more data centre is proposed for the suburb with another in Spotswood. Jemena says the new power poles are part of its local network upgrade "to help support Melbourne's growing energy needs". "These taller power poles are required mainly for safety reasons," said Michael Brear, a mechanical engineering professor at the University of Melbourne. "When you have a large electrical load like a data centre, you supply it most economically at a higher voltage than typically you would in your home. On streets where the poles have been installed in Melbourne's inner west, there is a strikingly consistent complaint: residents didn't know the change was happening. The power levels required for data centres mean old 7-metre wooden poles have to be replaced. ( ABC News ) In response to questions from 7.30, Jemena said: "We have heard feedback from residents and other stakeholders that our communication and engagement could have been better, and we are taking that feedback seriously." The company told 7.30 it has "paused works and [is] taking the time to listen to the community to understand their concerns". Paul Tyndale was one of those caught by surprise when Jemena crews disconnected his power in the inner west suburb of Spotswood to install a new taller pole. It was only then his family found out a new data centre was being proposed less than half a kilometre away. Paul Tyndale found out from a tradie that a new data centre was being proposed less than half a kilometre away from his home. ( ABC News: Norman Hermant ) "We found out about the data centre when the tradie who was disconnecting our house told my partner, 'This is for the new data centre,'" he said. GreenSquare, the company behind the proposed Spotswood Data Centre, now states on its website that the Spotswood poles are not part of its proposal and "are separate electricity network infrastructure works". On Sanderson Street in Yarraville, residents decided to fight back. After neighbours saw 15-metre poles go up a few blocks over, they knew their block was next. Residents on Sanderson Street saw the 15-metre poles going up nearby. ( Supplied ) On the day Jemena crews showed up in August, residents left cars and bins out to block equipment needed to install the poles. Some taped notes on car windows explaining the protest action. Residents on Sanderson Street left cars out to block the equipment needed to install the poles. ( Supplied ) "We were all just really caught off guard and just felt like it was really unfair that we weren't told about what was happening," resident Katrina Dardha said. Eventually, unable to get their equipment in position, the crews filled in the holes they had prepared for upgraded power poles and left. Milco Bogoevski (second from the right) and his neighbours staged a protest to stop the power poles from going up in their street. ( ABC News: Norman Hermant ) "Everyone decided this is not happening on our watch," resident Milco Bogoevski said. "If you stay quiet, it's at your own peril. I guess sometimes it takes something to make you really angry, to make you stand up." State Labor MP Katie Hall's seat includes West Footscray, home to a large NextDC data centre.
